   1|                                                                                    In Memoriam
   2|                                                                            Lance Douglas May
   3|                         Lance was born in Fitchburg and was a resident of Lunenburg for 69 years. He graduated from
   4|                         Lunenburg High School in 1968 and Mt. Wachusett Community College in 1971. He also at-
   5|                         tended Holy Cross College and Fitchburg State University. He worked for the Commonwealth
   6|                         of Massachusetts, Department of Revenue and the Department of Conservation and Recrea-
   7|                         tion. Throughout his life he was a devoted public servant to the Town of Lunenburg, serving
   8|                         on numerous boards and commissions. His public service began in 1971 when he was elected
   9|                        to the Park Commission at the age of 22. Lance's career continued to include the Board of Se-
  10|                        lectmen where he served as Chairman. He also served on the Lunenburg Housing Authority,
  11|                         Lunenburg Cable Advisory Committee, Lunenburg High School Athletic Hall of Fame Com-
  12|                         mittee and the Lunenburg Alumni Association. At the time of his death, he was the Chairman
  13|                         of the Lunenburg Cemetery Commission. Lance coached Little League baseball and soccer in
  14|                         town for many years. He was a former member of the Board of Trustees for Mt. Wachusett
  15|                         Community College and a longtime member of the Lunenburg Historical Society. Lance
  16|                         served as a former State Committeeman and Chairman of the Lunenburg Republican Party and
  17|                         worked on many campaigns. Lance was a member of the United Parish of Lunenburg, the Au-
  18|                        rora Lodge of Masons and was an Aleppo Shriner. He was a devoted family man and a true
  19|                         "Lunenburger" in every sense of the word.

   1|                                                                        LUNENBURG PROFILE
   2|                                                                       YEAR INCORPORATED- 1728
   3|                                                                         REGISTERED VOTERS-7870
   4|                                                                            FY'18 TAX RATE-$19.70
   5|                            OPEN TOWN MEETING GOVERNMENT- FIVE MEMBER BOARD OF SELECTMEN
   6|                                                    ANNUAL TOWN MEETING- IST SATURDAY IN MAY
   7|                                                   ANNUAL TOWN ELECTION- 3RD SATURDAY IN MAY
   8|                                                                        AREA- 26.63 SQUARE MILES
   9|                                                                          ROAD MILES- ABOUT 100
  10|                       Lunenburg was settled in 1718 and incorporated in 1728. It occupies a land area of
  11|                       approximately 26.4 square miles. Lunenburg is located in north central Massachusetts
  12|                       approximately 43 miles from Boston. It is bordered on the west by the Town of Ashby and the
  13|                       City of Fitchburg, on the south by the Town of Lancaster and the City of Leominster, on the east
  14|                       by the Town of Shirley, and on the north by the Town of Townsend.
  15|                       Local legislative decisions are made by an open town meeting consisting of all registered voters
  16|                       in the town. Subject to the legislative decisions made by town meeting, the affairs of the town
  17|                       are generally administered by a five member Board of Selectmen and a Town Manager. Local
  18|                       school affairs are administered by an elected seven member School Committee while local taxes
  19|                       are assessed by a three member Board of Assessors, all are appointed on an at-large basis for
  20|                       staggered three-year terms.
  21|                       Lunenburg is a semi-rural community located in northern Worcester County. Three water bodies
  22|                       account for somewhat of a clustered approach to the town's historical development. Lake
  23|                       Whalom and the former Whalom Amusement Park delineated the Whalom District from the
  24|                       remainder of Lunenburg. This district was developed as a housing base for many factory
  25|                       workers working in the mills and factories of Leominster and Fitchburg. In many ways the
  26|                       characteristics of the Whalom District more closely reflect characteristics of these cities than of
  27|                       the rest of Lunenburg. The Hickory Hills area of town, around Hickory Hills Lake, was
  28|                       developed as a private community comprised largely of vacation cottages.                                               The third body of
  29|                       water is Shirley Reservoir, a public water body also developed with mainly vacation cottages
  30|                       that have now been modified to year-round residences. Commercial and industrial development
  31|                       is permitted in several areas of town, primarily along the two major arteries (Routes 2A and 13),
  32|                       and the town's peripheries, due largely to the close proximity of Leominster's and Fitchburg's
  33|                       sewer and water systems. Although many farms and orchards had slowly developed into single
  34|                       family housing, farming continues on in Lunenburg. At the Annual Town Meeting on May 4th
  35|                       2013, the Town voted to establish an Agricultural Commission to represent, preserve, and
  36|                       enhance farming in the community and to administer the "Right to Farm" bylaw.
  37|                                                                                                6

===PAGE 18=== (ocr, 39 lines)
   1|                                                                                 REPORT OF THE
   2|                                                                                TOWN MANAGER
   3|                       The calendar year of 2018 was an eventful year for the Town of Lunenburg. The Town Manager
   4|                       and Board of Selectmen continue to work hard on serving the best interests of the Town and
   5|                       providing a high level of services while remaining fiscally responsible to the taxpayers. During
   6|                       2018 there were many topics addressed and accomplishments to highlight:
   7|                             • Increasing communication and outreach opportunities was a main theme throughout
   8|                                   2018. During the month of January 2018 the Town Manager launched a Town Facebook
   9|                                   page that was created as another means of getting information out to the public on
  10|                                   upcoming events, topics being discussed by local officials, public notices, and other
  11|                                  relevant information. At the request of other departments hoping to increase
  12|                                   communication to residents through social media, the Town Manager created a DPW
  13|                                   Facebook page in May and a Cemetery Commission Facebook page in November.
  14|                                   The Board approved the Other Post Employment Benefit (OPEB) policy drafted by the
  15|                                   Town Manager that designates 10% of the previous year's certified free cash be
  16|                                   deposited into the OPEB Trust Fund for this liability. This policy was created to continue
  17|                                  to put aside a conservative amount each year for the Town's growing liability that is also
  18|                                  recognized by bond rating agencies in terms of credit worthiness.
  19|                                   On January 9th the Board held a Complete Streets workshop to listen and learn from
  20|                                   attendees on their ideas for road projects that would improve accessibility for all modes
  21|                                   of transportation and all different ages and abilities in order to create a Project
  22|                                   Prioritization Plan under Massachusetts Department of Transportation's (MassDOT)
  23|                                   Complete Streets program. As part of the Complete Streets program, towns need to
  24|                                   create a Prioritization Plan, that is then reviewed by MassDOT, and if approved, makes
  25|                                   them eligible to apply for construction funding for projects on the plan. In July, the
  26|                                   engineering firm hired with a grant through the Complete Streets program, presented a
  27|                                   project Prioritization Plan that was adopted by the Board. This plan was submitted to the
  28|                                   MassDOT and was approved in September, which made the Town eligible to submit a
  29|                                  "Tier 3" project application for construction funding in the amount up to $400,000. In
  30|                                   September World Tech Engineering presented a project application that was submitted to
  31|                                   MassDOT in October for a request in the amount of $375,602. The Town received
  32|                                   notice that the grant was not approved in January of 2019 due to the large number of
  33|                                   applications and limited funding. However, the Town is eligible to continue applying for
  34|                                  this grant assuming funding from the State for this program continues.
  35|                       In February, the DPW and the Town Manager, working with the Town's Pay-As-You- Throw
  36|                       bag vendor WasteZero, began a retail distribution program so that PAYT bags transitioned from
  37|                       being ordered and sold by the DPW to the retail stores to the new model having retailers
  38|                       purchase directly and receive bags directly from WasteZero. The
  39|                                                                                               18

===PAGE 19=== (ocr, 35 lines)
   1|                                   goal of the program was to eliminate the need to monitor inventory and the liability of
   2|                                   having inventory on town premises.
   3|                             • The Town Manager presented a balanced budget for Fiscal Year 2019 to the Finance
   4|                                   Committee and Selectmen in mid-February for a total of $36,813,954.63. Part of the
   5|                                   Town Manager's recommendation was to continue to fund the Other Post-Employment
   6|                                   Benefits Trust Fund for the unfunded liability of retiree health insurance in the amount of
   7|                                   $100,000, continue funding the Special Purpose Stabilization Account for known large
   8|                                   capital items in the amount of $200,000, and fund the regular Stabilization fund in the
   9|                                   amount of $100,000. The FY2019 budget also included the hiring of an additional Full
  10|                                   Time Patrolman, an additional Full Time Firefighter, and Assistant Town Mechanic. The
  11|                                   Annual Town Meeting was held on Saturday, May 5*h and approved a total budget for
  12|                                   FY19 of $36,867,903.83.
  13|                                   As part of both the Town Manager and Board of Selectmen's goals surrounding
  14|                                   economic development, the Board endorsed an Economic Development survey in
  15|                                   February that was advertised on the town website, Town Facebook page, and hard copies
  16|                                   at town buildings.
  17|                                   Other business in February included an initial discussion on creating a Special Events
  18|                                   Permit. The discussion was continued at a meeting in June and then again in October.
  19|                                   Also in June, the Board discussed a proposed Noise Bylaw drafted by Police Chief
  20|                                   Marino and Town Counsel and discussed ongoing noise and safety concerns due to
  21|                                   visitors to Shady Point Campground on Lake Shirley. Later in the year, a proposed noise
  22|                                   bylaw was an article on the November Special Town Meeting warrant but was ultimately
  23|                                   defeated
  24|                             • During the month of March a group of 7" grade boys presented their idea of creating a
  25|                                   Skate Board park on town property to the Board of Selectmen. This project was borne
  26|                                   from a school program called "Genius Hour" where students meet weekly to develop an
  27|                                  idea. The students proposed raising funds through private donations in order to build the
  28|                                   park on public land. In April the Board voted to approve the proposed use of land to the
  29|                                   east of Kid's Kingdom and near the TC Passios building as the preferred option for a
  30|                                   future skate park. The Skateboard Park group provided monthly updates throughout the
  31|                                  year on their fundraising efforts and park design. At the end of year, the Board met with
  32|                                  the Parks Commission and Skateboard Park group about the scope of the skateboard park
  33|                                   and received additional input from the Parks Commission, who would ultimately be
  34|                                  responsible for the upkeep and maintenance of this park.

   1|                                   In March the Town Manager announced that after seeking quotes for optional dental
   2|                                  insurance for employees, the current provider, Altus Dental, responded with a significant
   3|                                  reduction to the monthly premium and rate guarantee for 2 years. The Selectmen signed
   4|                                   paperwork to refund general obligation bonds for roads and USDA Water and Sewer
   5|                                   Loans in order to save interest costs over the remaining term of the bonds.
   6|                                   As part of the March 2017 Air Quality Report, various improvements were made at the
   7|                                   Town Hall including cleaning of the HVAC system and the town records were removed
   8|                                   from the Town Hall attic and moved to the TC Passios building due to problems with bird
   9|                                   waste and weight of records in the attic.
  10|                             • The Town received District Local Technical Assistance for three projects that were
  11|                                   submitted by the Town Manager for the expansion of the "Formation of a Business/Town
  12|                                   Partnership" report, creation of a business brochure to promote the local economy and to
  13|                                   create a permitting guidebook to provide residents and businesses a guide to a
  14|                                   streamlined permitting process. Throughout the year the Town Manager and the Land
  15|                                   Use Director continued to hold "Business-Town Partnership" meetings that promoted
  16|                                   Lunenburg businesses to form a business association and ways the Town could help
  17|                                   promote local businesses such as the creation of the business brochure that was finalized
  18|                                   by the end of the calendar year. The brochure has been added to the Town website and
  19|                                  hard copies will be made available in the future. The Town Manager facilitated a
  20|                                  meeting of the Pepperell Business Association and the Lunenburg Business Association
  21|                                  that resulted in creating a regional business alliance that the Lunenburg Business
  22|                                   Association continued outside of the Town-Business Partnership meetings.
  23|                                   The Board authorized the final payment and signed the Massachusetts School Building
  24|                                   Authority paperwork to closeout the completion of the Middle/High School project.
  25|                            • This year was an incredible year for road projects in Lunenburg. Besides the
  26|                                   continuation of the $4M Pavement Management Plan on local roads, the Town was the
  27|                                  recipient of two major Transportation Improvement Projects through MA Department of
  28|                                   Transportation for the reconstruction of Summer Street and the milling and repaving of
  29|                                   Route 13/Chase Road. The Summer Street Road Reconstruction Project to perform
  30|                                  reconstruction of Summer Street through Lunenburg, Fitchburg, and Leominster was
  31|                                   awarded to Baltazar Contractors in March, who began the project in June and continued
  32|                                   construction throughout the remainder of the year. Funding for this project was realized
  33|                                  through a Transportation Improvement Project (TIP) and came after many years of
  34|                                   advocacy by prior Selectmen Paula Bertram and DPW Director Jack Rodriquenz. The
  35|                                  total award for this project was $7 million. At the end of the calendar year, the project
  36|                                   was ahead of the construction schedule. The Route 13/Chase Road project began and
  37|                                   was completed in 2018. The total award for this project was $1 million.

  13|                         received at this meeting included a majority of participants agreed that the old Primary building

  15|                         agreed that retaining the Ritter to lease, not sell, for small retail space or a restaurant was a

  19|                         the Eagle House, presented their findings. The goal of the property condition assessments was to
  20|                         identify the immediate and five year projection of repairs needed to those buildings by looking at
  21|                         the current condition and current use of the building, not the impact of changing the use of the
  22|                         building. Another goal for performing these assessments was to incorporate facilities capital
  23|                         projects into the Five Year Capital Plan that would assist in developing a long term facilities plan

   3|                       As of writing this report, it has been over two years since I was appointed your Town Manager
   4|                       and it is a responsibility that I take very seriously. The residents of Lunenburg demonstrate the
   5|                       true meaning of community that I have witnessed in various acts, whether it be supporting our
   6|                       local businesses, non-profit groups raising funds for those in need, or words of gratitude for our
   7|                       public safety and public works departments. I have the privilege of working with many talented
   8|                       individuals that are committed to helping the residents and business owners of Lunenburg and
   9|                       are consistently looking for ways to better serve the public. The accomplishments noted above,
  10|                       among the numerous day-to-day responsibilities, could not happen without the cooperation of
  11|                       dedicated staff, appointed, and elected officials that make the wheels of town government turn.
  12|                       Thank you to my Executive Assistant, Elaine Peterson, for all your hard work and keeping the
  13|                       office running smoothly. I would also like to thank the committee and board members,
  14|                       department heads and staff for the high level of service they provide to the residents of town.
  15|                       Specifically, I would like to express gratitude to the department heads that lead our various
  16|                       departments: James Marino, Police Chief; Patrick Sullivan, Fire Chief; Jack Rodriquenz, DPW
  17|                       Director; Karen Brochu, Town Accountant/Finance Director; Myleen Mallari,

  20|                       Herrick, Town Clerk; and all their staff for their talent and working together to make our town

   1|                                                  Architectural Preservation District Commission (APDC)
   2|                            2018 marked the first year that the APD bylaw was fully in effect. The APDC accepted and re-
   3|                           viewed six applications for construction in the district: at 920 Massachusetts Avenue, 99 Lan- caster,
   4|                           944 Massachusetts Avenue, 71 Highland, 136 Leominster, and 15 Oak. Two applications were like-
   5|                            for-like roof replacements, and the Committee considered ways to streamline the application process
   6|                           for such cases. Through the review of real and mock-applications, the APDC solidified its under-
   7|                            standing of the process and criteria for approval.
   8|                            Two cases of Demolition by Neglect were addressed: at 53 Lancaster and The Old Primary School.
   9|                            In the former case, volunteers were organized to clear vegetation away from the house and repair
  10|                            gutters. The owner was encouraged to move into assisted living. In the latter case, the APDC notified
  11|                            the Board of Selectmen and Town Manager of the violation.
  12|                            A warrant article came before town meeting to secure public funds for the demolition of the Old Pri-
  13|                            mary School. The APDC opposed the article and helped to defeat it.
  14|                            Chairman McGrath offered to volunteer his time and skills to restore the Old Town Pound in co-op-
  15|                           cration with the DPW. The project was still in planning stages at the end of 2018.
  16|                                                                     Building Department
  17|                          The Building Department is located on the second floor of the Ritter Memorial Building, 960 Massa-
  18|                          chusetts Avenue. Garry Rhodes serves as Building Commissioner and Lisa Normandin serves as the
  19|                          Administrative Assistant to the Building Department. Lisa also serves as the Administrative Assistant
  20|                          to the Zoning Board of Appeals. Andrew Hudson, Local Inspector resigned and will be missed.
  21|                          Building Permits for 2018 have increased slightly from 538 in 2017 to 544. Solar permits continue to
  22|                          be strong. We continue to see permits for weatherization which can be contributed to support provided
  23|                          by "Mass Save". In many cases Mass Save provides financial support to homeowners who upgrade
  24|                          insulation and do air sealing.
  25|                          The state of Massachusetts as of January 1s 2018 has now implemented the 9" Edition of the Building
  26|                          Code, CMR 780. The changes will impact both residential and commercial construction. The ninth
  27|                          edition is based on 2015 International Building Code.
  28|                          The Town Clerk issues Business Certificates. Before the Town Clerk will issue a Business Certificate
  29|                          you must first fill out a "Form of Intent". The "Form of Intent" is used to ensure that you will be in
  30|                          compliance with Lunenburg Zoning Bylaws. A copy of the "Form of Intent" can be obtained either
  31|                          online at lunenburgma gov or by coming by the Building Department Office. Once the form is re-
  32|                          viewed and signed by the Building Commissioner it can be presented to the Town Clerk.
  33|                          All 120 apartment units known as Whalom Luxury Apartments located off Whalom Road have been
  34|                          completed. Occupancy permits have been issued for all the building.
  35|                          Applications for Building, Electrical, Mechanical and Sheet Metal, Plumbing and Gas and Driveway
  36|                           permits can now be applied for online at lunenburgma. viewpointcloud.com. Hard copy forms to apply
  37|                           for these permits can be obtained on-line at lunenburgma gov or by stopping by at 960 Massachusetts
  38|                          during normal business hours.

   1|                                                                    CONSERVATION COMMISSION
   2|                       The Conservation Commission is a seven-member commission, appointed to 3-year terms by the Board of
   3|                        Selectmen, whose duties are codified under the Conservation Commission Act MGL Chapter 40 s 8C.
   4|                       The Commission enforces the Massachusetts Wetland Protection Act MGL Chapter 131 s 40 and Article
   5|                            The year 2018 was, as last year, one of a very busy and active agenda containing both public hearings
   6|                       and meetings for a wide range of projects from commercial development, subdivisions and small single
   7|                       family upkeep projects and larger scale industrial/commercial proposals along the Electric Avenue section
   8|                        of Lunenburg. The Conservation Commission worked to spell out goals of preparing to use 2019 to
   9|                       complete revising its regulations and land use policies to provide consistency with the original bylaw and
  10|                       to find those sections that may be out of date and need to be modified. This effort has been methodically
  11|                       approached and very comprehensive and is estimated to be completed by summer of 2019.
  12|                            The commission also held numerous inspections with the commission administrator on weekends prior
  13|                       to meetings to familiarize themselves with the upcoming proposals that would appear on their agenda.
  14|                       The commission continues to work with the Town on familiarizing itself with the upcoming stormwater
  15|                        mandates from the EPA and working towards compliance both by procedure and with any necessary
  16|                       codification as well as aiding with the community Notice of Intent to the EPA under the "MS4"
  17|                       regulations.
  18|                            The Conservation Commission implemented its forest stewardship planning after receiving grants
  19|                       noted on last year's annual report. These stewardship plans for five individual parcels will aid the
  20|                       commission in implementing environmental management plans which include timber stand management.
  21|                            This March, the commission bid and completed timber and environmental management in the small
  22|                       town forest. Other Conservation areas plans have been completed for the Lane property, the Large and
  23|                       Small Town Forests, the open space on Robbs Hill and the Cowdery. The commission retained Gary
  24|                       Gouldrup of New England Forestry Consultants, a noted forester with many years of experience working
  25|                       in Lunenburg and all of the adjacent towns/cities in this region serving those communities and private
  26|                       landowners. The Conservation Commission also held public recreational walks through its open space
  27|                       parcels and plans to continue to do so. The Commission has and continues to hold public forums on the
  28|                       implementation of its open space policies and timber-stand management. As a result of some of the
  29|                       meetings and forums held, the commission applied for and received funding from the Commonwealth to
  30|                       author a stewardship plan with a goal of enhancing bird habitat at the Hollis Road Conservation Area,
  31|                       developed under the DCR "Forestry for the Birds" program in partnership with the Massachusetts
  32|                       Audubon Society. The plan is being developed with a grant received from DCR.
  33|                           Copies of the current environmental stewardship plans are available on the Conservation Commission
  34|                       website at http://www.lunenburgma.gov/content/204/222/default.aspx
  35|                            The commission has also continued to work closely with Lake Shirley and Hickory Hills in the
  36|                       implementations of their management plans becoming actively involved in continuation of formulating
  37|                       updates designed to give a better picture of the overall health of the ecosystems and the various ways to
  38|                        ensure continued protection of these valuable resources.
  39|                            The commission thanks all the town agencies for a great year and looks forward to many more!
  40|                       Respectfully Submitted,

   1|                                                                               COUNCIL ON AGING
   2|                                                                            July 1, 2017 - June 30, 2018
   3|                       The mission of the Council on Aging is to advocate for the improved quality of life for all seniors through
   4|                       supportive services, programs and education. Councils on Aging were established under Massachusetts
   5|                       General Law Chapter 40, section 8B, to include setting policy for the administration of elder programs or
   6|                       services and to develop, coordinate and conduct such activities which advocate for elder issues.
   7|                        The FY18 Council on Aging staff consisted of Susan Doherty, Director; Amanda Koeck, Administrative
   8|                       Assistant and Transportation; Faith A. Anderson, Outreach Coordinator; Joanne Brazell, Meal Site
   9|                       Coordinator; Judy Alario and Elsa Watson, Meal Site Assistants; Jim McGuigan, Paul Grunditz,
  10|                       MART Van Drivers.
  11|                       Outreach Coordinator Faith Anderson retired in November 2017 and Pauline Roy was hired as the new
  12|                       Outreach Coordinator in December 2017. James Barrett was hired in February 2019 as a MART Van
  13|                       Driver.
  14|                        The Council on Aging Board is an eleven member board appointed to 3 year terms by the Lunenburg
  15|                        Board of Selectmen. The FY16 Council on Aging Board members were; Chairperson Pete Lincoln, Vice-
  16|                       Chairperson Jacquelyn Dwyer, Betty DiGiacomo, Sarah Grant, Brian Guenard, Deb Lincoln, Kevin
  17|                       McNally, Cheryl Moisan, Diane Nowd, Jane Rabbitt, and Judith Tarbell.
  18|                        The Town budget alone does not support this senior center. Other sources of funding are the Eagle House
  19|                       Supporters Inc., a non-profit 501c3 group, Formula Grant funding from the Commonwealth of
  20|                       Massachusetts, and Montachusett Regional Transit Authority.
  21|                        We are very lucky to have a large volunteer force at the Eagle House. In FY18 we had 48 volunteers who
  22|                       contributed 2,570.5 hours of their time to help us out by doing things such as driving for the meals on
  23|                       wheels program, program leaders, kitchen helpers, office help, library, and friendly visitors. We greatly
  24|                       appreciate their service.
  25|                       The Eagle House offers a variety of programs, such as health and wellness, arts and crafts,
  26|                       intergenerational, bocce, cards and games, cultural, information and referral, and social events both at the
  27|                       senior center and offsite. There were approximately 901 people who utilized the senior center in FY18.
  28|                       Those 901 people compiled 26,650 units of duplicated service by participating in the programs listed
  29|                       above.
  30|                       In FY18 the Council on Aging delivered 4,114 Meals on Wheels to 45 clients and provided 3,244 rides to
  31|                        68 clients on our senior van.
  32|                        We are very fortunate to have a Town Government that supports our center and understands the
  33|                       importance of supporting the Council on Aging to maintain quality services for our elders.
  34|                        Special thanks go to our 501c3 fundraising group, Eagle House Supporters Inc. This group provided
  35|                        funding for new living room furniture, office/kitchen supplies, various programs & entertainment, garden
  36|                       upkeep and spring mulch at the Eagle House Senior Community Center. Also special thanks to all of our
  37|                       outside agencies for donating time and programming to our clients.

===PAGE 63=== (ocr, 39 lines)
   1|                                                                  DEPARTMENT OF PUBLIC WORKS
   2|                                    The Department of Public Works combines the resources of the Highway, Park, Cemetery,
   3|                        Sewer, and Facilities divisions, and Vehicle Maintenance services into one department organizing
   4|                        and scheduling personnel and equipment to best serve the residents of the community through the
   5|                        effective delivery of an extensive scope of services with a high degree of efficiency.
   6|                                    "The mission of the Department of Public Works is to protect, preserve, and improve the
   7|                        Town's infrastructure and related assets in a manner which meets and exceeds the current and
   8|                        future social and economic needs of the community, to contribute to a healthy, safe and quality
   9|                        environment for the Town's residents and visitors, and to provide a cost effective and
  10|                        environmentally sound means of disposing of solid waste and wastewater."
  11|                                    Honesty and integrity are absolutes.                  They characterize the only forum in which anything
  12|                        worthwhile can be accomplished.
  13|                                    Make every effort to proceed correctly the first time. It may take a bit longer but will not
  14|                        require repeated attempts.
  15|                                   Loyalty up and down the chain of command is essential to success.
  16|                                    Every employee is essential. Those at the top are support people. The real work is done by
  17|                        the men and women who drive the trucks, operate the equipment, turn the wrenches, and provide
  18|                        a seamless flow of paperwork.
  19|                        DEPARTMENTAL OBJECTIVES
  20|                                    Public Works is either working or on call twenty-four hours a day three hundred and sixty-
  21|                        five days a year to respond to any weather, infrastructure, roadway, or facility related emergency
  22|                        that may arise.
  23|                                    We strive to enhance the awareness of the value Public Works provides to our Town, and
  24|                        ensure others are aware of our contribution. This is not for an expectation of praise, but rather to
  25|                        make sure efforts are not forgotten as they merge into the fabric of our everyday expectation of
  26|                        service.
  27|                                    Major events, particularly in the form of devastating storms, over the past years have
  28|                        highlighted the fact that Public Works has a seat at the table and is a major player in emergency
  29|                        management. Town Officials, Police, and Fire acknowledge that Public Works is critical in order
  30|                        to facilitate the required services of others. We must continue to build on this awareness.
  31|                                    This department must also reach out to the public we serve and educate them to the fact
  32|                        that the common services they receive do not just happen, but rather are the efforts of a dedicated
  33|                        staff of individuals, service companies, and vendors. Safe roadways, wastewater control, solid
  34|                        waste collection and recycling operations, tree removal, storm water management facilities and
  35|                        grounds maintenance, winter snow and ice removal, cemeteries and parks are the expected services
  36|                        supporting everyone in the community.
  37|                                    We will continue to engage the public in order to set reasonable expectations and gather
  38|                        support for annual budget requests, capital requests, and specific projects.
  39|                                                                                               63

===PAGE 64=== (ocr, 41 lines)
   1|                         DEPARTMENTAL GOALS FOR FISCAL 2020
   2|                                         • Continue to coordinate administrative directives with the activities of all public
   3|                                               service departments and organizations within the DPW to improve service levels.
   4|                                         • Coordinate with those who work daily in Town facilities to best prioritize capital
   5|                                              improvements.
   6|                                         • Increase involvement with our insurance provider to make better use of available
   7|                                               resources in an effort to obtain credits toward lessening premiums.
   8|                                         • Set realistic expectations. Make clear through public education that due to limited
   9|                                               resources, particularly in the area of personnel, the level of service provided by
  10|                                               Public Works is not always optimal.
  11|                                         • Work diligently to establish and maintain a high level of courteous communication
  12|                                               and interaction between members of all boards and commission.
  13|                         PAVEMENT MANAGEMENT
  14|                                     It has become a high priority goal of the BOS as Road Commissioners, to achieve a
  15|                         pavement condition of 72%-75% Town-wide. Although State funded Chapter 90 funds remains
  16|                         stagnant, the dedicated Pavement Management line in the operational budget has grown
  17|                         substantially.
  18|                                    Results of the Comprehensive Pavement Management Plan displayed clearly the inequity
  19|                         of the distribution of paving funds toward higher use main and collector roads leaving local
  20|                         neighborhoods unattended. Using the PMP as evidence, residents went to the polls to vote
  21|                         favorably on a four-million-dollar debt exclusion targeting exclusively the local roads. Expending
  22|                         approximately a million dollars in the initial year, and in excess of a million the following year has
  23|                         resulted in a major enhancement of road conditions.
  24|                                    The debt exclusion funding combined with state and operational funds has nearly tripled
  25|                         the total paving value of years past as we attack a nine-million-dollar backlog of repairs.
  26|                                    Our pot hole log has and is expected to lessen exponentially as new paving increases, a
  27|                         clear benefit of the dollars expended. There is much work yet to do but expectations are high.
  28|                         FLEET MAINTENANCE
  29|                                    The DPW is responsible for the repairs and preventative maintenance to all Town vehicles
  30|                         and equipment. High performance police units, first responder Fire and Rescue apparatus, park,
  31|                         cemetery, and school vehicles as well as over 30 pieces of highway related machinery are serviced
  32|                         by department personnel. Outsourcing of highly technical repairs has become more frequent and
  33|                         therefore costlier. Due to the volatile global oil market, the overall cost of fuel and petroleum based
  34|                         products continues to be a moving target and therefore difficult to estimate annually.
  35|                                    The installation of a vehicle maintenance software program continues to be a valuable tool.
  36|                         Each repair is logged by department and vehicle identification number and memorialized in a data
  37|                         bank. Every vehicle can be tracked for part numbers, required services, as well as frequency and
  38|                         cost of repairs over the life of the equipment. As Director I have developed and submitted to Town
  39|                         Officials a vehicle replacement schedule based upon that created by the American Public Works
  40|                         Association in order to more clearly represent our capital needs.

  10|                                A facilities staff of one individual remains on-call 24 hours a day 365 days per year.
  11|                        Staff attempts to keep buildings compliant with current codes to insure a safe secure work
  12|                        environment. Any significant interruption of service within Town buildings carries the potential
  13|                        of disrupting or disabling necessary services provided to the community. The facilities support
  14|                        staff are problem solvers and technicians with a wide range of experience encompassing all of the
  15|                        construction trades. Together with a stable of reliable professionals they deliver services or oversee
  16|                        those functions provided by specialized subcontractors. Unfortunately, the creation of a capital
  17|                        replacement program has fallen short of expectations. Years of neglect have created a significant
  18|                        backlog of necessary repairs and improvements. The process has become reactionary at best. The
  19|                        Building Reuse Committee reported clearly that asset management relative to our buildings
  20|                        requires a professionally prepared assessment and a long range capital plan. To this end our plan
  21|                        for 2020 is to procure the services of Project Management Consultant to survey, quantify, project
  22|                        building needs and establish an annual cost. Public Works continues its use of a building
  23|                        maintenance software program as a framework for day to day activities. Requests for service are
  24|                        acknowledged immediately, prioritized, and completed in a timely manner. Those individuals
  25|                        requesting service are contacted upon completion of the tasks and a history of the repair is filed
  26|                        electronically.
  27|                        ENVIRONMENTAL
  28|                        Storm Water
  29|                                    As a component of the aforementioned "debt exclusion" approximately five hundred
  30|                        thousand dollars of the four million in total has been earmarked for storm drainage including but
  31|                        not limited to repair of the existing collection system, and additional construction.
  32|                                    As roadways are scheduled for pavement, drainage is surveyed and necessary repairs are
  33|                        addressed to avoid paving over problems. New Federal and State storm water regulations will
  34|                        likely force the Town to become more proactive albeit with no additional identified source of
  35|                        funding.
  36|                                     At the conclusion of winter and again in the late fall drainage structures in close proximity
  37|                        to open water are cleaned and inspected. Public Works maintains an aggressive schedule of street
  38|                        sweeping and catch basin cleaning, the front line of storm water management.
  39|                        Waste Water
  40|                        The DPW continues as the caretaker of the entire sewer system. Day to day maintenance of the
  41|                        overall wastewater system inclusive of 10 pump stations is outsourced to a specialty
  42|                                                                                               65

===PAGE 66=== (ocr, 43 lines)
   1|                                   vendor but continues to be the responsibility of Public Works. Business management,
   2|                        inspections, and permitting, remain in-house and the responsibility of the DPW.
   3|                         Tree Removal
   4|                                    Storm damage together with the natural attrition of every species creates a backlog of tree
   5|                        felling and pruning that far exceeds the allotted budget. The department is unable to fulfill each
   6|                        resident request and must prioritize work based upon the calculated degree of danger to residents
   7|                        and property. With the establishment of a Hazardous Tree Survey, a more efficient approach to
   8|                        defects has been established through prioritization. Sadly, the amount of work far exceeds the
   9|                        available revenue. Until there is a substantial infusion of funds, the DP W will act in a reactionary
  10|                        mode. All work aside from brush removal, chipping, and the felling of small diameter trees is
  11|                        outsourced due to the necessity of a bucket truck or crane and a licensed professional. Each spring
  12|                        DPW staff initiates the activity of removing and disposing of woody debris within the right-of-
  13|                        way together with a Town-wide program of curbside mowing. An aggressive program by our
  14|                        energy provider in recent years has lessened the burden of the Town to remove those trees that
  15|                        may cause an interruption of electrical service to the community.
  16|                        Landfill
  17|                                   The "capped" landfill off Young's Rd. remains in compliance with the inspection protocol
  18|                        mandated by the Division of Environmental Protection. The site is monitored regularly for
  19|                        excessive methane gas as well as the possibility of groundwater contamination.
  20|                                   The frequency of the testing, reduced through a special permit, acquired as a result of
  21|                        consistently favorable results, remained constant throughout the year. The landfill site including
  22|                        the perimeter fencing is inspected on a regular schedule by DPW personnel.
  23|                                    Adjacent to the "cap" is a storage area for catch basin materials and street sweepings both
  24|                        determined by the EPA to be hazardous waste. We are allowed to store these materials through the
  25|                        procurement of a (BUD) Beneficial Use Determination permit. The DEP requires yearly testing of
  26|                        these materials. Other communities are required to transport these tainted materials to an
  27|                        appropriate site at an excessive cost.
  28|                                   On weekends during the fall and springtime months DPW personnel oversee and manage
  29|                        the annual composting of brush, leaves and other organic debris providing a valuable service to
  30|                        our residents and add a valuable component to our recycling program. There has to date been no
  31|                        dedicated funding toward the organization or long range remediation of this area. With water and
  32|                        sewer at the perimeter this acreage has been proposed as a potential recreational area for the Town.
  33|                        As of yet this project has not gained traction.
  34|                        Solid Waste
  35|                                   In the past, Public Works would have the responsibility to monitor, order, store, and
  36|                        distribute trash bags in order to facilitate the curbside collection of trash and recyclables by our
  37|                        current vendor, Casella Inc. Pay as you throw... Recently we entered into an agreement allowing
  38|                        our "trash bag" supplier to coordinate the effort between supplier and vendor resulting in some
  39|                        mixed reviews.
  40|                        Lake Shirley Dam
  41|                                  In the early 1990's, with the structure in need of repair/rebuilding The Lake Shirley
  42|                        Association turned over ownership of the dam to the Town. After completion of a total
  43|                                                                                               66

===PAGE 67=== (ocr, 40 lines)
   1|                       reconstruction, responsibilities for maintenance, monitoring, and record keeping was completed
   2|                       solely by a small number of volunteers from the Lake Association. In 2004-2005 custodianship of
   3|                       the dam, compliance with State dam regulations, the establishment of an operations manual as well
   4|                       as an emergency action plan was placed under the umbrella of the Department of Public Works.
   5|                       As with the storm water program and other EPA / DEP mandates compliance with current and
   6|                       future regulations is critical. We rely on the expertise and support of a professional consultant to
   7|                       assist with predetermined mandates. The most recent inspection resulted in a positive report.
   8|                       Winter Operations
   9|                                  Snow and ice present a major challenge to our Town. The safety of the general public
  10|                       depends on the ability of the DPW to maintain our roadways to a high level of safety despite the
  11|                       severity or the duration of snow and ice events. To that end we have developed a winter operations
  12|                       procedure based upon a detailed plan with a flexibility to accommodate the unpredictability of
  13|                       each storm. The expectation of immediate service is high and must be delivered to every part of
  14|                       Town in a timely manner.
  15|                                  Departmental preparedness begins with successful implementation of the capital plan.
  16|                       Financial support is necessary to provide effective fleet rotation insuring minimal interruption of
  17|                       services due to breakdowns and repairs. In the fall, material is delivered to the Chase Rd. facility.
  18|                       Lunenburg is in a consortium with 14 other communities in an effort to procure the lowest possible
  19|                       price for road salt, an absolute necessity. From late summer to early fall vehicle maintenance staff
  20|                       inspects and prepares the trucks, spreaders and plows for winter operations. During the
  21|                       construction season road crews address right-of-way issues, overhanging branches, and pavement
  22|                       defects in order to eliminate obstacles to snow removal. Each division within the DPW is involved
  23|                       in winter operations. Typically, DPW staff combines with up to 18 subcontractors to provide
  24|                       service.
  25|                                  Generally, it is not the amount of snow but the duration of the event that determines the
  26|                       overall cost. For example, a fast moving snow storm of 6-8 inches will cost significantly less than
  27|                       a long duration freezing rain event even though the accumulation is much less. Historically, the
  28|                       department operates in a deficit due to a yearly allocation that is below the cost of an average
  29|                       winter.
  30|                                   It is a dedicated group of individuals who successfully challenge the worst Nature has to
  31|                       offer regardless of severity or duration.
  32|                                                                "DPW workers are the original Storm Troopers"

  36|                       available as required, much of the Town-wide landscape maintenance is outsourced, resulting in
  37|                       significant savings and increased efficiency over an in-house operation. Repair of the multi-use
  38|                       track complex is imminent. After many years, a mutual effort between the Commissioners and all
  39|                       users of the facility is gaining traction.

   1|                                                                         FINANCE COMMITTEE REPORT
   2|                                                            Lunenburg Finance Committee Report, Fiscal Year 2019
   3|                       The Town Budget to be presented for approval is balanced, consistent with the Town's fiscal policies, and reflects
   4|                       recognition that future needs must be addressed. Department Heads have presented 'level service' budgets, and requests
   5|                       beyond level service. Based on the financial forecast and funding opportunities, the Town Manager is proposing increases
   6|                       beyond level service in historically high need areas, such as police and fire. An assistant mechanic position, which had
   7|                       been removed to address past fiscal challenges, has been returned to the Department of Public Works.
   8|                       The Town is now in the position to add services to Public Safety through 1 Police Officer and 1 Firefighter/EMT. There
   9|                       is a recognized need to continue to grow Public Safety as the Town and population demographics continue to change.
  10|                       The Town also remains committed to incorporating steady increases (tied to motor vehicle excise tax increases) in the
  11|                       Pavement Management Plan to ensure that recent improvements paid for through debt exclusion will be adequately
  12|                       maintained going forward. $50,000 of the DPW budget increase addresses this.
  13|                        As we attempt to manage costs associated with the roads, the Town has also begun to set aside monies for other
  14|                       infrastructure and building needs by establishing and funding a Special Purpose Stabilization Fund. This budget deposits
  15|                       $200,000 into that fund.
  16|                       Debt Service continues to decrease. The debt for the purchase of a fire engine will be retired during the coming fiscal
  17|                       year. This makes room for short term borrowing within the general budget to help replace the aging ladder truck, which
  18|                       has been on the Capital Planning radar for quite some time. The new debt will not hit the budget until 2020, so is not
  19|                       reflected in the budget presented here, but is planned for going forward.
  20|                       The Town has made several changes to Health Insurance plans over the past few years that have helped keep increases
  21|                       low. This year, the increase in premiums is coming in at about 7 percent, which affects both the 'Unclassified' portion of
  22|                       the budget, and the School Department budget. A growing portion of Health Insurance costs is coverage for retirees. To
  23|                       address this growing liability, the Town is continuing to fund the OPEB Trust Fund, this year depositing $100,000 for
  24|                       post-employment Health Insurance payments.
  25|                       The Retirement Assessment has gone up more than 10 percent. Town employees pay into 1 of 2 retirement systems.
  26|                       Licensed school district employees contribute to the Massachusetts Teacher Retirement System, which requires no
  27|                       additional town funding. Any additional funding of this Retirement System is done at the State level, and is reported in
  28|                       notes to the Town Financial Statements as an 'On Behalf' payment. Non licensed school personnel and Town side
  29|                       employees contribute to the Worcester County Retirement System. The Town makes two payments to this system, an
  30|                       employer contribution for active employees and an assessment to fund the 'Unfunded Liability' of future payments to
  31|                       retirees. It is the future liability assessment that is driving the increase.
  32|                       The total budget presented incorporates the following changes:
  33|                              • General Government is increased $64,780, including salary adjustments, and technology
  34|                                  increases.
  35|                              • Central Purchasing has no change.
  36|                              • Police is increased $113,408 including salary adjustments and a new police officer position.
  37|                              • Fire is increased $112,498 including salary adjustments, a new firefighter/EMT and
  38|                                   overtime.
  39|                                                                                               69

   1|                             • Radio Watch is increased $20,749
   2|                             • Total Protection, which includes Police and Fire, is increased $256,468, or 8.7%, which still
   3|                                  leaves a gap to catch up to the growing needs of the town, an ongoing priority.
   4|                             • DPW is increased $79,207 adding $50,000 for pavement management as planned along with
   5|                                  salary increases and the return of the assistant mechanic position.
   6|                             • Buildings and Facilities is decreased, but that is from the adjusted budget at last year's
   7|                                  Special Town Meeting which identified funds to make needed repairs and fund a full survey
   8|                                  of maintenance and repair needs of several Town buildings.
   9|                              • Solid Waste is increased $3,130, following a large decrease made the previous year.
  10|                             • Health & Sanitation is increased $2,491.
  11|                             • Council on Aging is increased $5,694, which moves some funding for MART van scheduling
  12|                                  to the town ahead of anticipated reductions in formula reimbursements from MART.

  23|                             • Retirement Assessment is increased $114,832, about twice as much as last year.

  31|                        continued service. We are grateful for the continued cooperation of the Town Manager, each
  32|                        department head, and other Town Boards and Committees to ensure that every budget question is
  33|                        answered.

   1|                                                                        HISTORICAL COMMISSION
   2|                           The Historical Commission consists of five appointed volunteers who meet once a month from
   3|                         September to June. The work of the Historical Commission is preservation and appreciation of
   4|                         all things historic in the Town of Lunenburg. The Historical Commission has through the past
   5|                         year been represented on the Architectural Preservation District Commission by two of our
   6|                         members, Richard McGrath and Cullen Dwyer. The design standards for the APDC have been
   7|                         completed.
   8|                          The Bronze Marker project has been completed, which was made possible through the efforts of
   9|                         Joshua Herrick of Troop 1728 Lunenburg and his Eagle Scout Project. All the houses in
  10|                         Lunenburg's National Registered Historic District were surveyed for National Registered
  11|                         Historic plaques (last available in 1987) and those home's missing plaques were purchased by
  12|                         the Historic Commission from the Erie Landmark Company. Installation was completed and
  13|                         finally all the houses in our National Registered Historic District will get the recognition they
  14|                         deserve. Recognizing our Nationally Registered houses will be an ongoing effort of the
  15|                         Historical Commission with both ongoing registration and providing plaques to houses that meet
  16|                         the criteria.
  17|                           Our second marker project is nearing completion with the purchase of the Arnold & Litch
  18|                         family cemetery marker from the Erie Landmark Company. This will mark a small family
  19|                         cemetery plot that was lost to neglect on West Street. The installation of this marker will be this
  20|                         spring.
  21|                           We continue to hold hearings and enact the Demolition Delay Bylaw of the Town of Lunenburg
  22|                         for the destruction of Historic properties. The Demolition Delay Bylaw had the delay expanded
  23|                         to 18 months at the Fall 2018 Town Meeting. We are involved in preservation efforts for 1755
  24|                         House at 68 Elm Street, which is under demolition delay. This house was known as the Battles
  25|                         House and Benjamin P. Redington who owned it in 1790, served in the Revolutionary War and
  26|                         mustered from Lunenburg.

  17|                              • To provide children with open access to all digital resources and media and to ensure that

  19|                              • To continually evaluate, increase/update non-fiction collection to present an accurate,
  20|                                    updated collection for children of all ages and to optimize shelving of this collection for
  21|                                    ease of access

  23|                                    a life-long love of reading.

  26|                         2018. The amount of hours read for the 2018 Summer Reading Program increased from 447
  27|                         hours read in 2017 to a whopping 4,163.5 hours read! Program participation ran strong with 188
  28|                         tweens and teens attending 11 programs.
  29|                         A teen Dungeon's and Dragon's club was started in September to coincide with the start of
  30|                         school. While there is only one official library D&D night, the group of 14 meet twice a week in
  31|                         the teen room to play their various campaigns, trading off the Dungeon Master (leader) position.
  32|                         Sessions range from as small as 4 players to as large as 14 depending on the teens' availability
  33|                         that day. This program has been immensely popular and continues to grow.
  34|                         The teen room has been updated and refurnished to make the space meet the needs of today's
  35|                         teens. White board table with outlets to charge their phone was added in addition to relocating
  36|                         the TV to have a designated video game area where more teens could comfortably gather. New
  37|                         shelving for both books and board games was added as well.

   1|                          LUNENBURG PUBLIC ACCESS (PAC)
   2|                            FY1               Mission: Develop, modernize, establish and operate the
   3|                                              Town of Lunenburg's Public and Government (P&G) Access
   4|                               8             Channels to reflect what matters to Lunenburg
   5|                         Public Access Cable Committee (PACC)
   6|                         Steve Walker, Chair
   7|                         Faith Beall, Vice Chair
   8|                         Jeff Bajko, Secretary
   9|                         The Lunenburg Public Access Cable Committee (PACC) is responsible for the long-term plan to manage
  10|                         the Public Access Channels available to the Lunenburg community through Comcast, the town's only cable-
  11|                         service provider.
  12|                         The overall strategy includes providing and improving equipment to acquire, record, broadcast and re-
  13|                         broadcast programming from both town functions and meetings, as well as programming from publicly
  14|                         available sources.
  15|                         Programming
  16|                         CH9 - Public
  17|                          Public Access Cable (PAC) produced 57% of the local programming on Ch9 in FY18, down 18% from
  18|                         75% in FY17. The decrease in local programming was largely due to the lack of volunteers and paid
  19|                          videographers.
  20|                         Local programs included high school sports, band concerts and school events, just to name a few. The
  21|                         remaining 43% of programming was obtained through other media sources (Access Share) and online
  22|                         downloads (MassAccess and PEGMedia).
  23|                                                                                               77

   4|                           Several categories of local programming were provided on Ch9, among the top were Infor-

   6|                          Informational provided subscribers with unique presentations and overviews that helped
   7|                          to familiarizes them with local resources and information.

  15|                          is for the promotion of the Council on Aging's Eagle House and their services to the Senior

   5|                          Contract Renewal
   6|                          Contract negotiations with Comcast began in FY18 to renew the agreement between Com-
   7|                          cast and the Town of Lunenburg commencing on March 1, 2018 through February FY28.
   8|                          The Cable Committee, Tom Alonzo, Steve Walker, Paula Bertram, advised by IT Director
   9|                          Steve Malandrinos and Town Manager Heather Lemieux, worked with KP Law to reach a
  10|                          mutually acceptable contract with Comcast. The result of the negotiations, finalized in June
  11|                          of FY18, brought an increase in franchise fees from 2.5% to 5.0%, and a capital infusion of
  12|                          $170,000 over 3 years. The first of these payments of $85,000 was made on June 27, 2018.
  13|                          The next 2 payments will be $42,500 in FY19 and FY20 respectively. Capital payments are
  14|                          being held in an Undesignated Fund (Comcast Tech Capital Grant) revenue account for fu-
  15|                          ture capital use. Additionally, it was agreed to provide Lunenburg with a 3'° Channel exclu-
  16|                          sively for educational content to be available within 24 months of the contract effective
  17|                          date.
  18|                          PACC reserved the Comcast infused capital of $85,000, along with the $39,796.01 already in
  19|                          the Undesignated Fund from 2008, for a total of $124,796.01. These monies can be used
  20|                          for a future studio and various other capital equipment needs.
  21|                          In FY20 the PAC financial structure is planned to change to an enterprise fund for all reve-
  22|                          nue and expense related activity.
  23|                          Legal Expenses related to contract negotiations accounted for 11% of the FY18 expenses.

   7|                          Summary
   8|                           The support of the local community has helped Lunenburg Public Access (PAC) succeed. PAC has received
   9|                           numerous requests for recording, as well as positive viewer feedback. People are watching. In fact, the
  10|                           viewership of the Government Channel (Ch8) alone, on-air and YouTube, shows a solid commitment to Public
  11|                           Access as a valuable resource for local information.
  12|                           The Public channel (Ch9) added new and unique programming for all to enjoy as well. While local program-
  13|                           ming on Ch9 decreased in FY18, it is expected to increase in FY19 with the addition of videographers and stu-
  14|                           dio productions. But we can't do this alone. Volunteers and community involvement is necessary for PAC to
  15|                           grow. Individuals are urged to bring their ideas and talent forward to help create programming. Training and
  16|                           guidance is provided for those who are interested.
  17|                           With the infusion of capital from the Comcast contract, PAC can now make necessary improvements moving
  18|                           forward. It will allow for the addition of more videographers and the capital equipment necessary to in-
  19|                           crease quality and content. Better technical support will also be possible with the hiring of a Production Engi-
  20|                           neer in FY19.
  21|                           PAC is proud of the accomplishments made in FY18. However, there is much more work to be done. Admin-
  22|                           istrative and production needs are continually increasing, videographer demands are great, and technical
  23|                           requirements are always at the forefront. Careful planning and budgeting has lead to success this year, as
  24|                            well as the solid commitment to Lunenburg.

   1|                                                            SENIOR PROPERTY TAX WORK-OFF PROGRAM
   2|                                                                                          Est. 1998
   3|                                                      CALENDAR YEAR JANUARY 1, 2018 - NOVEMBER 1, 2018
   4|                          The Property Tax Work-Off Committee is a five-member committee appointed by the Lunenburg
   5|                          Board of Selectmen.
   6|                          2018 Committee Members:
   7|                          *Sheila Craigen
   8|                          *Susan Doherty
   9|                          *Nancy Forest
  10|                          *Robert Hamel
  11|                          *Myleen Mallari
  12|                          The Lunenburg Property Tax Work-Off Program offers income eligible senior citizens age 60+ an
  13|                          opportunity to receive up to $1,000 off of their property tax bill in the calendar year rather than the
  14|                          fiscal year. Participants worked in various town departments to earn the tax abatement doing general
  15|                          office duties, custodial, library shelving, Meals on Wheels, and kitchen assistance.
  16|                          For each hour worked a person received $10 and worked up to 100 hours between January 1, 2018
  17|                          and November 1, 2018 to receive the abatement. Any hours worked beyond that were considered vol-
  18|                          unteer hours.
  19|                          There were eight Lunenburg residents who participated between January 1, 2018- November 1, 2018.
  20|                          These individuals, as a whole, accumulated 771.25 hours ($7,712.50) towards their abatements.
  21|                          Eligibility Requirements:
  22|                          *Applicants must be 60 years of age or older
  23|                          *Own and occupy a home in Lunenburg as their primary residence for at least one year
  24|                          *Receive a property tax bill in their name or their spouse's name who is also 60 years of age or older
  25|                          *Meet the income guidelines of : One person household - $40,000 / Two person household - $60,000
  26|                          *All new applicants are required to have a CORI background check and must re-apply and be accept-
  27|                          ed annually for participation in the program.
  28|                          Earnings are exempt from state taxes only. Earnings are subject to federal and FICA tax withholdings
  29|                          and are also subject to OBRA if participants are not receiving a pension from either Worcester Re-
  30|                          gional Retirement or Massachusetts State Teachers Retirement.
  31|                          Departments who participated between January 1, 2018- November 1, 2018:
  32|                          *Lunenburg Treasurer/Tax Collector
  33|                           *Lunenburg Board of Health
  34|                          *Lunenburg Building Department/Zoning
  35|                          *Lunenburg Council on Aging
  36|                          *Lunenburg DPW/Sewer Departments
  37|                          *Lunenburg Public Library
