   1|                                                                           SEWER COMMISSION - FY18
   2|                              The five member Sewer Commission was originally established at the Special Town
   3|                              Meeting on May 6, 2006. At the May 20, 2017 election, Joe Anderson and Joan Pease
   4|                              were re-elected to 3 year terms and Troy Daniels was elected to the one-year term as a
   5|                              write-in to fill out the 3-year term vacated by Richard St. Cyr who resigned from the
   6|                              Commission in February of 2017. Usually held the first Sewer Commission meeting after
   7|                              the May Town election when the Commission elects the officers for the new fiscal year,
   8|                              the election of officers for FY 18 did not occur until August 2017 due to Charter discus-
   9|                              sions and meeting attendance. On August 15, 2017, Joe Anderson was elected as Chair-
  10|                              man, Carl Luck as Vice-Chairman, and John Reynolds to serve as Clerk. Troy Daniels
  11|                              chose not to run for re-election in May 2018 and Ryan Stober was elected to serve on the
  12|                              Sewer Commission in May 2018. We welcome Ryan and thank him for his willingness
  13|                              to serve on this Commission.
  14|                             The Sewer Commission bears the responsibility of overseeing the Sewer Enterprise
  15|                             Fund, planning for the future, and developing and implementing rules, regulations and
  16|                             policies. Under the Town's Charter, responsibility for the day-to day operation, care and
  17|                              maintenance of the sanitary sewers are under the supervision of the Town Manager who
  18|                              delegates the responsibility to manage and maintain the operational side of the system to
  19|                              the Department of Public Works' Director, Jack Rodriquenz. The Town of Lunenburg
  20|                              does not operate a sewer treatment plant. Approximately 74% of Lunenburg sewer is dis-
  21|                             charged to the City of Leominster, and the other 26% is discharged to the City of Fitch-
  22|                              The Sewer Commission continued contracting with Small Water Systems Services
  23|                              (SWSS) for the Operations and Management of the 10 pumping stations, emergency
  24|                              generators and sewer infrastructure. The Sewer Commission has been very satisfied
  25|                              with the personnel, the work and the arrangement with SWSS, renewing the contract
  26|                             for a second three-year term in July 2016. In FY18, we completed the 5th year with
  27|                             Small Water as our contractor for the supervision of the town's sewer system.
  28|                              There are currently 882 properties connected to the Lunenburg system and another 374
  29|                             which have access to Town Sewer but are not yet connected. During FY 18, 27 new ac-
  30|                              counts connected to Town Sewer. The Commission billed out $792,898 in quarterly
  31|                             sewer bills, and had $61,985 of prior year delinquencies added to the owners' property
  32|                              tax bills for non-payment. Six properties were assessed a privilege fee in FY18. One
  33|                              property assessed was residential. Three assessments were for 24-unit apartment build-
  34|                             ings, and 2 other properties were commercial buildings. Privilege fees help to pay down
  35|                             the debt owed by the Town on the original sewer project.
  36|                              Throughout FY18, the Commission worked on several policies, including Grease Trap reg-
  37|                              ulations, Connection Charges, and Irrigation and Manual meter policies. The Commission
  38|                              worked with several vendors in preparation for upgrading the irrigation meters currently in
  39|                              use. Current technology would allow the meters to be read by radio or cellular commu-
  40|                              nication. Investigations are still underway to find the best fit for our customers while try-
  41|                             ing to keep replacement costs low as well.
  42|                             In July of 2017, the Commission began a very satisfactory relationship with the new Town
  43|                              Counsel, Mead, Talerman and Costa and specifically Adam Costa, who has been of great
  44|                              assistance to the Commission throughout the year. He was especially helpful during
  45|                             FY18 as the Commission grew more familiar with the State's Open Meeting Law and as-
  46|                              sisted in the work to establish Communication guidelines. The Sewer Commission contin-
  47|                             ued its work in FY18 to identify and reduce Inflow and Infiltration (I/I), working with the
  48|                              engineers at Weston & Sampson. In December 2017, with their assistance, the
  49|                                                                                               85

===PAGE 86=== (ocr, 50 lines)
   1|                            Sewer Commission filed their "Infiltration/Inflow Control Plan" with the State as required
   2|                            by the Department of Environmental Protection. The Commission worked with Weston &
   3|                            Sampson to accomplish the 2018 manhole rehabilitation project in the hopes to decrease I/I
   4|                            where there were known issues. Reducing I/I continues to be the focus of the Commission
   5|                            going into FY19.
   6|                            The Commission has continued with the annual permit program for the 20 Food Service
   7|                            Establishments with grease traps and interceptors on Town Sewer. Throughout FY 18,
   8|                            the Commission worked with multiple establishments in correcting their non-compliance.
   9|                            The "Rules & Regulations for Oil & Grease Traps/Interceptors for Food Establishments"
  10|                            continues to be a focus of the Commission as Fats, Oils and Grease (FOG) can negative-
  11|                            ly affect the smooth operation and maintenance costs of the sewer system. While the
  12|                            Grease Trap Regulation focuses on commercial and public disposal, individual home
  13|                            owners can also contribute a significant amount of grease into the system which increas-
  14|                            es everyone's costs. Whether on sewer or septic, grease should not be put down the
  15|                            Throughout FY 18 the Commission met with several different groups regarding Sewer Ex-
  16|                            tensions, specifically at Cross Rd, Lancaster, Upland, and Tilton Ave. The Commission is
  17|                            always willing to discuss a potential sewer extension when the applicant can show that
  18|                            challenges exist for standard septic systems.
  19|                            At the May 2018 Town Meeting, the Commission put forward 3 articles, 2 of which related
  20|                            to the FY19 budget and stabilization funds. For the standard budget article for FY19,
  21|                            $705,301.08 was appropriated from Sewer Enterprise revenues and the sum of
  22|                            $156,869.92 was appropriated from Retained Earnings for a total appropriation of $
  23|                            $862,171.00 to operate the Sewer Enterprise Fund for FY19. The amount of $883,369.58
  24|                            was approved to cover both the Enterprise Fund's share of Town services and debt service
  25|                            on the sewer betterments. The second article transferred monies to the Capital Reserve
  26|                            Stabilization Fund in the amount of $29,000, approximately 3% of proposed revenues as
  27|                            the Commission had done for FY 18. This fund is to be used to maintain and improve the
  28|                            operating efficiency of the system or cover large emergency expenditures. A main goal of
  29|                            the Sewer Commission continues to be maintaining a balanced budget every year without
  30|                            having to raise rates for our customers. This is the fifth year that the operating budget has been
  31|                            balanced without a rate increase to the users. The third warrant article was to add Tilton Ave-
  32|                            nue to the Sewer Service AreaSSA) for future sewer extension requests, having been
  33|                            omitted when the Sewer Bylaw and original Sewer Service Area map was accepted by the
  34|                            Town at the May 2009 Town Meeting. All three articles passed at Town Meeting and
  35|                            Tilton Ave. was added to the Sewer Service Area. It was determined at the time of this
  36|                            Annual Town Meeting that any contributions to Stabilization Funds based on income re-
  37|                            ceived for their purposes would be acted on at the Special Town Meeting following the
  38|                            close of the fiscal year. The two funds affected by this change are the Sewer Bank-Inflow/
  39|                            Infiltration Stabilization Fund and the Reserve Capacity Stabilization Fund. A portion of
  40|                            the connection charges assessed at the time of an application for permit to connect go into
  41|                            these accounts and target resolving 1/1 issues and future capacity costs paid to the cities of
  42|                            Fitchburg and Leominster for increased capacities.

===PAGE 87=== (ocr, 18 lines)

   1|                                                                               BOARD OF HEALTH
   2|                          The Board of Health Office is located in the old Ritter Library building on the corner of Mass. Ave
   3|                          and Leominster Road. Our office is on the upper level at the end of the hall on the right. We can be
   4|                          reached at 978-345-4146, extension 430.
   5|                          The Board of Health, with the assistance of its agent, the Nashoba Associated Boards of Health, con-
   6|                          tinued its mission to maintain its focus on public health and safety issues during 2018, reviewing Title
   7|                          V Inspection Reports, building permits, septic and well permits, nuisance investigations, housing in-
   8|                          spections, complaints and general public health related issues as well as resident concerns.
   9|                          The Board of Health oversees the Septic System Repair Program which helps low to moderate income
  10|                          families replace failed septic systems or connect to public sewer. Anyone interested in finding out
  11|                          more about this program can contact the Board of Health office.
  12|                          Homeland Security planning is ongoing. Meetings continue between our agents, other Town Depart-
  13|                          ments and regional entities to develop a plan for not only Lunenburg but with our partner towns in our
  14|                          region.
  15|                          This year, we processed applications for Septic Permit Lot Tests, permits for new construction, new
  16|                          wells, repairs or upgrades to septic systems and well permits. The Board continues its vigilance with
  17|                          regard to septic systems, wells, food service inspections, housing and nuisance complaints and its gen-
  18|                          eral mandate to protect the environment and groundwater of the Commonwealth.
  19|                          The Board of Health provides numerous other services in cooperation with our Health Agents, the
  20|                          Nashoba Associated Boards of Health. In addition to our environmental services, numerous clinics are
  21|                          provided throughout the year to our residents. These clinics provide inoculations, including Flu Shots,
  22|                          Blood Pressure screenings, Well Oldster Clinics and Dental screening. Fluoride treatment and dental
  23|                          checks of our youngsters in the School System are provided by the Nashoba dental staff.
  24|                          The Town of Lunenburg participates in the Central Mass. Mosquito Control Project. Mosquito Con-
  25|                          trol monitors the mosquito population in Lunenburg and advises of any potential diseases such as EEE
  26|                          and West Nile Virus and sprays frequently to control the population during the warmer times of the
  27|                                       Residents who want to have their property sprayed can do so by emailing to:
  28|                          cттcp@cmmcp.org, calling (508) 393-3055, completing a request on their webpage at: http://
  29|                          www.cmmcp.org, or calling the Board of Health office. This service is free of charge to residents.
  30|                           With our Nashoba Nursing and Hospice partners we provide in home visits to ill residents recovering
  31|                           trom illness and hospice care and counseling to those in need of this service.
  32|                          Please contact our office in the Ritter Building for more information.
  33|                          Please remember that our Board Members volunteer their time and efforts on behalf of you, the Citi-
  34|                          zens of Lunenburg.
  35|                          If you have something that you think we can help you with, we are at your service. Contact the Board
  36|                          office at 582-4146 ext. 430.

   2|                                                                               FIRE DEPARTMENT
   3|                              CHIEF                                                                                                             655 Massachusetts Ave
   4|                           Patrick A. Sullivan                                             UNCHAURO MAKE.                                       Lunenburg, MA 01462
   5|                           TEL: (978) 582-415 FAX: (978) 582-403:
   6|                          The Firefighters and Emergency Medical Technicians of the Lunenburg Fire Department are dedicated
   7|                         to providing the highest quality, most cost effective fire and emergency medical services to the citizens
   8|                                                                              of the Town of Lunenburg.
   9|                                    In 2018 your Fire Department responded to 1942 calls for service, broken down as follows:
  10|                                     Fires & Hazardous Conditions                                       452                    Emergency Medical 982
  11|                                    Inspections                                              506                   Other                          33
  12|                                     2018 saw one of the greatest changes in the history of the Lunenburg Fire Department with
  13|                         the achievement of 24 hour staffing in the Station. On August 6th,                         ", 2018 Firefighters Timothy Downey
  14|                         and Austin Flagg were promoted to Career Firefighters and joined the existing 4 members as Full Time
  15|                         Staff.
  16|                                     Current Fire Department staffing is now 7 Career and 40-45 On Call Firefighters and Emergen-
  17|                         cy Medical Technicians, plus 1 full time Administrative Assistant/EMS Coordinator. The Station is
  18|                         EMT Monday-Friday from 8am-4pm. This coverage is a combination of Full Time personnel in con-
  19|                         junction with 88 hours per week of per diem coverage. The per diem coverage is provided by our Call
  20|                          Firefighter/EMT's manning the Station at their hourly rate.
  21|                                    The call volume in 2018 was a slight overall decrease over 2017, however we. We also expe-
  22|                         rienced a 6% increase in Emergency Medical related calls, which is consistent with the growth we
  23|                         have seen over the last 10 years.
  24|                                    We currently operate two Ambulances at the Advanced EMT Level, but must rely on outside
  25|                         agencies for assistance with full Advanced Life Support (Paramedic Level) Care. The first steps to-
  26|                         wards achieving our own Paramedic service were taken in 2018 with FF Downey beginning training as
  27|                         a Paramedic. It is planned that FF Flagg will begin the training in 2019. These two members, plus ad-
  28|                         dition of 3 more Firefighter/Paramedics over the next 3-4 years will allow us to provide service to the
  29|                         community at the full Advanced Life Support Level. Hiring Paramedic Level trained Firefighters and
  30|                         equipping the ambulances to that level will bring a higher level of care to our residents in a faster,
  31|                         more efficient way.
  32|                                     Though we have achieved 24-hour coverage in the Station, many EMS calls and nearly all fire
  33|                         calls still require more personnel than are on duty in the Station. This means we still rely heavily on
  34|                         the dedication and commitment of our Call Firefighters and Emergency Medical Technicians. Our Call
  35|                          personnel remain, and will remain for the foreseeable future a vital part of our emergency response.
  36|                                                                                               96

===PAGE 97=== (ocr, 43 lines)
   1|                                      A new Call Firefighter/EMT must attend over 340 hours of initial training, plus additional
   2|                          time in orientation and field training. Members qualifying to drive Fire Apparatus must complete an
   3|                          additional 65 hours of classroom and practical training. On average, it takes a new member one and
   4|                          a half to two years to properly complete these requirements. Unfortunately, for a variety of reasons
   5|                          we often do not retain members for more than 5-6 years.
   6|                                     In 2018, the Fire Prevention Division conducted 506 Inspections. This is in addition to multi-
   7|                           ple fire drills and public education initiatives. By law, we are required to inspect Smoke and Carbon
   8|                           Monoxide Detector installations when a home is sold, as well as all new oil burner and propane gas
   9|                          installations. Any business holding a liquor license is also required to be inspected for fire safety
  10|                          issues as well. In addition, all new construction projects must have their plans reviewed for proper
  11|                          fire protection, as well as ongoing inspections during the construction process. Personnel also con-
  12|                          tinue to provide fire safety education to not only children in our schools but adults as well. Other
  13|                          Fire Safety Initiatives undertaken during 2017 include:
  14|                                      Continuation of a Department of Fire Services Grant in the amount of $6953 to assist with
  15|                          Fire Safety Education in both the Schools and with Senior Citizens. This Grant provides funding for
  16|                          both materials and personnel to bring fire safety education to our most vulnerable populations.
  17|                          Highlights of activity through this grant include:
  18|                                      Educational programs in basic fire safety in Grades K-3, including use of the Regional Fire
  19|                          Safety Trailer.
  20|                                      Educational programs in conjunction with the Council on Aging. These included cooking and
  21|                          heating safety, a CPR Demonstration and Ice safety.
  22|                                      Participation in the Senior Center's "Sand for Seniors" Program. This program provides
  23|                          buckets of walkway sand for Senior Citizens who were unable to obtain it for themselves in the win-
  24|                          ter months. In partnership with this program, Captain James Ricci delivers the sand to the residents
  25|                          and when possible, inspects their homes for Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors. If the resident
  26|                          was lacking detectors, Capt. Ricci is able to install free detectors obtained through the Senior SAFE
  27|                           Grant.
  28|                                     It should be noted that each year, 50% of fatal fires are found to have nonfunctional or non-
  29|                          existent smoke detectors.
  30|                                     During 2018, Call Firefighters Robert Barrett, Melissa Buchanan, Ronald Hyatt and Lorenzo
  31|                          Leonardo graduated from the Massachusetts Firefighting Academy's Call/Volunteer Training Pro-
  32|                          gram. This intensive 4-month program provides the basic skills firefighters need to operate in to-
  33|                           day's challenging environments. All newly hired Firefighters are required to complete this program
  34|                          within one year of hire. In addition, Firefighter Barrett received the Martin McNamara Award for
  35|                           Outstanding Achievement in his Recruit Class. This award, named after a Lancaster Firefighter killed
  36|                          in the Line of Duty is award to the overall top student in each Call/Volunteer Recruit Class.
  37|                                     I would also recognize Call Firefighter Timothy Paton. Tim retired from the Department,
  38|                          after 34 years of service to the community.
  39|                           Apparatus replacement continues to be a concern. The replacement for our 30-year-old Ladder
  40|                          truck has been ordered and is expected in the late summer or early fall of 2019. This unit is ex-
  41|                           pected to serve the town for 25+ years. The next oldest unit in the fleet, Engine 4 has been sub-
  42|                           mitted for replacement on the FY' 20 Capital Plan.
  43|                                                                                               97

===PAGE 98=== (ocr, 43 lines)
   1|                                     This 1995 vintage unit was our primary pumper from its delivery up until 2015. It has served
   2|                          the town well but has seen increasing maintenance costs and downtime due to wear and tear. In
   3|                         late 2018 the unit's pump failed, necessitating costly repairs just to return it to operational condi-
   4|                          tion. Rescue 2, a 2008 Ambulance has also been submitted for replacement as it is near the end of
   5|                         its projected life span. The high reliability required of front line emergency apparatus becomes in-
   6|                          creasingly difficult to maintain as these units reach the end of their life span. It hoped that due con-
   7|                          sideration will be given to replacing both units.
   8|                                    In conclusion, I would like to thank the members of the Lunenburg Fire Department for their
   9|                          outstanding commitment to the Town. Their enthusiasm, professionalism and dedication continue
  10|                          to impress me every day. I would also like to thank the other department heads, boards and com-
  11|                          missions for their continuing help. Most people do not realize the level of interdepartmental coop-
  12|                          eration that occurs in the daily course of town business. My thanks also go out to the citizens of
  13|                         Lunenburg for their ongoing support of public safety. It is that support that allows us to continue
  14|                         providing the services you expect from us.

   2|                                                                                     Lt. Michael Luth
   3|                                                                               Officer Whitney Mansfield
   4|                          Lt. Mike Luth began his career in law enforcement with the Town of Tyngsboro as a patrol officer. He was
   5|                          soon elevated to the rank of Sergeant. Mike left the Tyngsboro Police Department to take a job with the Se-
   6|                          cret Service during the Clinton and Bush administrations. Having a passion for small town policing Mike
   7|                          settled in Lunenburg taking a patrol officer position in 2004. Mike was promoted to the position of Patrol Ser-
   8|                          geant and eventually to Administrative Lieutenant and second in command. He commanded many positions
   9|                          including the Court Liaison officer, training coordinator, public records and liaison to the Council on aging
  10|                          where he taught self-defense and Senior drivers just to name a few. Mike was responsible for organizing the
  11|                          Citizen's Police academy, and managed the College Internship programs. Mike left the Lunenburg Police De-
  12|                          partment when he accepted the Position of Chief of Police in the Town of Groton, where he currently resides.
  13|                          Mike will be missed around the Police Station, but we are extremely proud of his accomplishments and we
  14|                          wish Chief Mike Luth the best of luck.
  15|                          Whitney Mansfield was first introduced to the Lunenburg Police Department as a Fitchburg State University
  16|                          Criminal Justice Intern. Whitney was immediately found to be highly motivated, kindhearted individual with a
  17|                          high degree of integrity, and one who had a keen interest in Law Enforcement. She was immediately taken in
  18|                          by the organization and offered a sponsorship to the Reserve Intermittent Police Academy. Whitney attended
  19|                          the academy and was quickly offered a position within our Reserve ranks. She was appointed as a Reserve
  20|                          officer shortly after graduating from the academy in July of 2017. Whitney quickly became an outstanding
  21|                          candidate for a position as a full time police officer. Whitney applied and received a full time position with the
  22|                          Bedford New Hampshire Police Department and is currently in training. Whitney will make of fine police
  23|                          officer. She will certainly be sorely missed but we are very proud of her and wish her the best of luck with her
  24|                          new career.
  25|                                                                     About the Police Department
  26|                          The Police Department is in operation 24 hours a day 7 days a week. The department is staffed with the Chief
  27|                          of Police supported by the Public Safety Coordinator, and one Administrative Lieutenant. Three Sergeants/
  28|                          Shift commanders, one of the Sergeants presently assigned to K-9/Traffic enforcement, nine Patrol Officers
  29|                          and 11 Reserve Intermittent Patrol Officers make up the patrol unit. Supporting the patrol unit is the Criminal
  30|                          Investigation Unit headed by a Detective Sergeant. Within the C.I.U. is the School Resource Officer who is also
  31|                          assigned to Community Outreach, and who is accompanied by Hank the Therapy dog. The Lieutenant and
  32|                          Public Safety Coordinator are on duty Monday thru Friday between the hours of 7Am and 3Pm. Office hours
  33|                          for the Chief of Police are 8Am to 4Pm Monday thru Friday.
  34|                          The Animal Control Officer responds to domestic animal calls on a 24 hour 7 day per week basis. The public is
  35|                          reminded to report any animal related complaints to the Regional Call Center at (978) 582-4531. For emer-
  36|                          gencies, dial 911. More information can be found on the Animal Control Web site at lunenburgma.gov.
  37|                          Dogs must be licensed by April 1St annually. Dogs must have a current Rabies certificate to qualify for licens-
  38|                          ing. This can be done at the Clerk's office in Town Hall, 17 Main Street Lunenburg, MA 01462. Unspayed Fe-
  39|                          male/Unaltered Male $20 fee. Spayed Female/Altered Male $5 fee. Late Fee: $25
  40|                          The front desk is open Monday thru Friday from 7AM to 7PM. Emergency, Non-emergency and 911 calls are
  41|                          routed through Nashoba Valley Regional Dispatch District, (NVRDD). For all emergencies, dial
  42|                          911. For general calls, please call (978) 582-4531.
  43|                          Applications for Firearms Licensing can be found on the Police Department Website at lunenburgma.gov.
  44|                          Contact (978) 582-4531 for an appointment.

===PAGE 102=== (ocr, 45 lines)
   1|                                                                 The State of the Police Department
   2|                           The Police responded to 19383 calls for service this year, a 13.7% increase over last year; responded to 315
   3|                           motor vehicle accidents, investigated 1070 incidents, 47 Field Interview Reports, wrote 1889 motor vehicle
   4|                           citations, arrested 144 people, summonsed 207, and placed 8 people in protective custody. The K-9 was de-
   5|                           ployed 27 times. In the first half of fiscal 2017, staff assignments had to be increased 75 times to effectively
   6|                           meet service demands.
   7|                           The day shift desk officer answered 1741 calls and took 1407 lobby inquiries and complaints between July and
   8|                           December of 2018. The day shift desk officer wrote 94 incident reports in 2018. This year the day shift desk
   9|                           watch officer was responsible for conducting suicide watch and assisting with the court processing of 83 de-
  10|                           tainees; either taken into custody overnight or during the day shift. The day shift desk officer processed 154
  11|                           Firearms Licenses, 17 Non FID related fingerprints, and registered 16 Sex Offenders. The 3pm to 7pm desk
  12|                           watch officers assisted in the processing of, 50 detainees while providing suicide watch and numerous other
  13|                           services including providing support for the patrol staff.
  14|                           Calls for service, which will continue to rise, are affected by, not only growth in our community, but the sur-
  15|                           rounding communities as well. Traffic too will continually increase and will have a direct effect on the amount
  16|                           of traffic accidents the police will have to investigate. Environmental factors too play a role in the motor vehi-
  17|                           cle accident picture. Incidents and arrests amounts are affected by social and economic factors.
  18|                           I again emphasize the important of keeping with current growth trends. Growth invariably plays a major role
  19|                           in Police Calls for Service, arrests, incidents and motor vehicle accidents. The demands for police services will
  20|                           continue to rise and the police department will have to grow in kind.
  21|                           Calls for service have increased by 13.6% over last year. Incidents have declined by 16.5%. Incidents are cases
  22|                           that do not necessarily result in an Arrest, but require a report and investigation. Arrests are down by 2.9%,
  23|                           with motor vehicle accidents increasing by 17.15%.
  24|                           Group A crime against Persons are down this year. These crimes include; Rape, Statutory Rape, Aggravated
  25|                           Assault, Simple Assault, Intimidation, Kidnapping/Abduction.
  26|                           Group A crimes against Property is up 9% this year. Crime against Property include; Burglary/Breaking & Enter-
  27|                           ing, Larceny, Shoplifting, motor vehicle theft, Forgery, Fraud, stolen property, destruction of property, vandal-
  28|                           ism.
  29|                           Group A crimes against Society have increased by 16%. Crimes against Society include; Drug crimes, Pornogra-
  30|                           phy/Obscene Material, Weapons law violations.
  31|                           Group B crimes have declined by 21% this year. Group B crimes include; Bad checks, Disorderly conduct, Driv-
  32|                           ing under the influence, Drunkenness, Family nonviolent offenses, Liquor Law Violations, Trespassing, and all
  33|                           other offenses.
  34|                           Lunenburg is a safe community to live in thanks in large part to citizen input. Reporting crime is key to the
  35|                           safety of a Town such as ours. The Police cannot provide effective protection without the citizen involvement.
  36|                           I encourage every citizen to report crime as it occurs, without hesitation, as a timely response is vital to the
  37|                           successfully outcome of any police investigation. "See something, say something."
  38|                           Thank you again this year for allowing me to manage your Police Department. The necessary funding to sup-
  39|                           port my request to bring police staffing to a level that will keep up with the demands of growth has been over-
  40|                           whelming. I ask you to please continue to support our initiatives. The police department endeavors to deliver
  41|                           the service the public expects and is entitled to.
  42|                           Respectfully Submitted
  43|                           Chief James P. Marino
  44|                           Chief James P. Marino

   1|                                             Ad Hoc Open Space Advisory Committee to the Planning Board
   2|                           The Open Space Committee's efforts in FY'18 revolved around updating the town's expired Open Space and
   3|                           Recreation Plan. The Plan was drafted in accordance with Massachusetts Executive Office of Energy and Envi-
   4|                          ronmental Affairs Division of Conservation Services' (DCS) guidelines and is intended to direct Lunenburg's
   5|                           efforts to improve and enhance its open space and recreation resources. The Plan is the culmination of many
   6|                           months of volunteer work, built with input from all corners of town government and, most importantly, its resi-
   7|                           dents. It is not only comprehensive in its scope, but is also measured in its objectives and attainable in its goals.
   8|                           The Plan has been submitted to DCS for review and, once approved, will make the town eligible for DCS-
   9|                           administered grant programs through 2026.
  10|                           Partly driven by the Open Space Plan update, the Planning Board also expanded and modified the composition
  11|                           of the committee. We are now comprised of seven members instead of five, with one representative each from
  12|                           Planning, Conservation, and Parks and four at-large members. The diverse representation allows for greater
  13|                           collaboration and communication among related land use boards around matters of conservation and recreation
  14|                          interest.
  15|                           Finally, the Open Space Committee continued its role in reviewing Chapter 61 withdrawals notices for their
  16|                           potential open space and recreation value to town and advising other municipal boards of the same.

   1|                                                                          Lunenburg Public Schools
   2|                                                                        Superintendent's Message
   3|                          It is a pleasure for me to present my first annual report for the Lunenburg Public Schools.
   4|                          This report reflects some of what I have learned about the promises and needs of a district I
   5|                         am proud to lead. During the last 6 months, I have been executing my Entry Plan. I have
   6|                          conducted forums and one-on-one interviews. I have reviewed many documents. I have at-
   7|                         tended numerous school and community events and activities. I have been able to observe
   8|                          the district processes and procedures, tour the facilities and grounds, and most importantly,
   9|                         spend time in classrooms observing teaching and learning. While there is much to be proud
  10|                          of, there is also good work to be done to improve the efficiency of operations, strengthen
  11|                         curriculum and instruction, and support all learners.
  12|                         I want to acknowledge that this community has demonstrated its support for the schools by
  13|                         supporting two building projects in the last 15 years. The Lunenburg Primary School and
  14|                         Lunenburg Middle/High School are beautiful, modern facilities for teaching and learning.
  15|                         A modern facility is; however, but one factor in providing students with a quality education.
  16|                         Rigorous programming designed to meet the academic, social and emotional needs of all of
  17|                         our students is foundational to a quality learning experience. In addition to meeting a stu-
  18|                         dent's basic needs, we must ensure that the curriculum is well-designed; materials are avail-
  19|                         able to implement that curriculum; and that teachers have the knowledge and skills requisite
  20|                         for effective instructional practice. All of this must be supported by the use of data to assess
  21|                         and monitor student learning. Today's classrooms also require the seamless integration of
  22|                         instructional technology to create engaging lessons, provide differentiated instruction and
  23|                         assessment, and facilitate analysis of achievement data to monitor the growth and support
  24|                         the success of all of our students.
  25|                         I also want to acknowledge that I have experienced a collaborative approach to planning and
  26|                         problem-solving with the Town Manager, Heather Lemieux. I am very grateful for that. I
  27|                         appreciate the effort on the part of the School Committee and the Board of Selectmen to
  28|                         strengthen communication and find opportunities to work together. I trust that, working
  29|                         together, we will be able to find ways to meet the needs of the children of Lunenburg.
  30|                         Through my transition, the district continues to be focused on implementation of the District
  31|                         Strategic Plan (2018-2023). Our Strategic Goals are:
  32|                         Goal 1: Social-emotional learning, prevention programs and secure schools provide safe
  33|                         environments, promote kindness and celebrate cultural differences.
  34|                          Goal 2: Civic learning and engagement enable all students to become knowledgeable citi-
  35|                          zens and active community members.
  36|                          Goal 3: Curricula and assessments in major subject areas are aligned with recent Massa-
  37|                         chusetts State Frameworks and fully implemented.
  38|                          Goal 4: Implementation of digital literacy and computer science curriculum is expanded;
  39|                         and, instructional technologies are more available.
  40|                          Goal 5: The processes for annual professional development ensure opportunities for well-
  41|                         targeted individual, school-based, and district-wide professional growth.
  42|                          Goal 6: Strategies to improve instructional support for struggling learners are enhanced.
  43|                          Goal 7: Enrichment opportunities are expanded to include the arts and other areas of high
  44|                         student interest.
  45|                          Goal 8: Collaboration and communications within and among the schools and the commu-
  46|                         nity are improved.
  47|                                                                                              110

===PAGE 111=== (ocr, 33 lines)
   1|                          As evidence of continued progress on these goals, we are revising our social studies and his-
   2|                          tory curriculum to align with the new Massachusetts History and Social Science Curriculum
   3|                          Framework; providing professional development at the Primary School in literacy as part of a
   4|                          Department of Elementary and Secondary Education (DESE) literacy grant; providing pro-
   5|                          fessional development in behavioral interventions and supports, and building a strong school
   6|                          culture. We have created district-wide leadership in these areas with the creation of a Behav-
   7|                          ioral Health Advisory Council, Elementary Literacy Team, and Professional Development
   8|                          Committee.
   9|                          The MCAS data analysis conducted at the district leadership level indicates a need for con-
  10|                          tinued focus on curricular and instructional supports in order to increase the achievement and
  11|                          growth of our Students with Disabilities subgroup. Grades 4 and 5, require resources and
  12|                          focus on essay writing, specifically on conventions, text types and purposes. In grades 3 and
  13|                          4, we need to target instruction on multiplication and fractions; and in grade 6 on equations
  14|                          and inequalities.
  15|                          This year DESE implemented a new accountability system. The new system still allows the
  16|                          DESE to identify schools requiring assistance or intervention, as well as those demonstrating
  17|                          success. Highlights of the new system include: (1) the inclusion of additional accountability
  18|                          indicators; (2) a focus on raising the performance of each district's or school's lowest per-
  19|                          forming students in addition to the performance of the district or school as a whole; and (3)
  20|                          the discontinuation of accountability and assistance levels (Levels 1 to 5).
  21|                          Under the new accountability system, annual performance determinations for districts and
  22|                          schools will be calculated using Indicators: English language arts (ELA), Mathematics, and
  23|                          Science achievement; ELA and Mathematics mean student growth percentile (SGP); four-
  24|                          year cohort graduation rate, extended engagement rate, annual dropout rate; student progress
  25|                          towards attaining English language proficiency; chronic absenteeism, percentage of 11th &
  26|                          12th graders completing advanced coursework.
  27|                          Indicators are weighted. Substantial weight for achievement, growth, English language pro-
  28|                          ficiency, and graduation rate indicators are required by federal law. Federal law also requires
  29|                          that these indicators combined should have much greater weight than the additional indica-
  30|                          tors. Under the new accountability system, the weighting of achievement and growth is based
  31|                          on ratios instead of percentages, maintaining the achievement to growth ratio of 3 to 1.
  32|                          Thing at delor she the Accountabiliy of the district and school balowing the 2018

   7|                       expected to continue to have additional asbestos removal planned for a number of years. A request
   8|                       for $162,000 for FY20 was submitted into the town's capital planning process to abate the second

   1|                         Indicator 12 - Early Childhood Transition. This indicator measures the % of children referred
   2|                         by Part C, found eligible for special education services, and who have an IEP developed and
   3|                         implemented by their third birthdays. The state target for this indicator in 100% and Lunenburg
   4|                         is noted as "Suppressed". Data is suppressed if the number of students referred by Part C and
   5|                          found eligible for special education services is fewer than 10.
   6|                         Indicator 13 - Secondary Transition. In all years, the state target for Secondary Transition is
   7|                          100%. This indicator measures the % of youth with IEPs aged 16 and above with an IEP that
   8|                         includes appropriate measurable postsecondary goals that are annually updated and based upon
   9|                         an age appropriate transition assessment, transition services, including courses of study, that
  10|                         will reasonably enable the student to meet those postsecondary goals, and annual IEP goals
  11|                          related to the student's transition services needs. Lunenburg was last reviewed in this area in
  12|                          2015-2016 and was 100.0% in compliance.
  13|                         Indicator 14 - Post-School Outcomes for Students with IEPs. This indicator measures the %
  14|                         of students with IEPs who exited high school during the 2015-2016 school year and self-
  15|                         reported post-school engagement in education or employment one year after leaving high
  16|                         school. Engagement is defined through three measurements:
  17|                               • Measurement A: Enrolled in higher education within one year of leaving high school.
  18|                               • Measurement B: Enrolled in higher education or competitively employed within one year
  19|                                    of leaving high school.
  20|                               • Measurement C: Enrolled in higher education, or in some other postsecondary education
  21|                                    or training program; or competitively employed, or in some other employment within
  22|                                    one year of leaving high school.
  23|                         Measurements are cumulative with Measurement C reflecting the total number of exiters
  24|                         engaged in a post-secondary activity one year after leaving high school. For the 2016-2017
  25|                         school year, state targets for the three measurements of Post-School Outcomes are Measurement
  26|                          A: 51%; Measurement B: 86%; and Measurement C: 93%. Lunenburg rates are as follows (from
  27|                         reporting year 2014-15): Measurement A = 50%, Measurement B = 75%, and Measurement C
  28|                         = 75%.

  23|                                                                           Lunenburg Primary School
  24|                           The Lunenburg Primary School is an early childhood education center for students in preschool to
  25|                           second grade. Our students range from three years old to eight years old. Our school community
  26|                           is made up of students, teachers, parents and support staff working together to maintain a learning
  27|                           environment that focuses on the academic and social emotional needs of the whole child.
  28|                           The October 1, 2018 student enrollment reported to the Department of Elementary and Secondary
  29|                           Education was 422 students. Currently our Preschool program services 48 three and four year old
  30|                           students. We have six Kindergarten classes servicing 147 students. Class sizes in our
  31|                           Kindergartens are at 24-25 students. This year we have five grade one classrooms servicing 115
  32|                           students with class sizes between 21-24. Five second grade classrooms have 119 students with
  33|                           class sizes ranging from 23 to 25 students.
  34|                           Our professional development has centered on literacy instruction this year. In early October we
  35|                           received notification from Governor Charles D. Baker that the school was awarded a FY19 Early
  36|                           Grades Literacy grant of $6,520. This grant funded teacher participation in an extensive
  37|                           professional development opportunity that included three statewide literacy institutes and follow-
  38|                           up regional meetings. We explored the development of language in young children (birth-9); the
  39|                           role language plays in literacy; and the content of the Massachusetts ELA/Literacy Framework
  40|                           Standards for Language.
  41|                                                                                              119

===PAGE 120=== (ocr, 40 lines)
   1|                        Teachers discussed strategies to engage early grades students in reading, writing, talking, and
   2|                        thinking about the content they are learning in order to promote language development. The grant
   3|                        team shared information with grade level teams throughout the year. In September and November,
   4|                        the general and special education teachers participated in two full day Project Read workshops
   5|                        focused on phonics. Project Read applies sound/symbol knowledge to spelling and reading
   6|                        comprehension using targeted multisensory activities and direct instruction. This professional
   7|                        development was designed to enhance the instruction we provide for K-2 students each day at
   8|                        school.
   9|                           The Primary School is a Title One school and we have continued our tiered instructional system
  10|                        to insure that all students have the services they need to be successful. Common assessments are
  11|                        completed in the fall, winter, and spring for all children in grades K-2 in the areas of reading,
  12|                        writing, and math. These common assessments serve to monitor the effectiveness of teacher
  13|                        instruction and the progress of students. Struggling students are identified for additional support
  14|                        in Reading, Math, Speech, Occupational and Physical Therapy.
  15|                        Our staff works to maintain a school culture which is positive, inclusive, and supportive of each
  16|                        of our members. This year we have collaborated with Dr. Curt Bates of Seaside Educational
  17|                        Consultants to identify strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats in our school practices and
  18|                        culture. He is guiding us to focus on a few areas that can really enhance our overall school culture.
  19|                        The Primary School Council meets each month to discuss school related concerns. Serving as an
  20|                        advisory group to the principal, the council is charged with reviewing the school building budget
  21|                        and developing the school improvement plan.

  11|                                                                  Turkey Hill Elementary School
  12|                       Turkey Hill Elementary is now in its third year as a 3-5 building. There are currently 372 students,
  13|                       with 121 third graders, 115 fourth graders, and 136 fifth graders. We employ 24.5 teachers, 100%
  14|                       of whom are licensed in their assignment area. Our student/teacher ratio is 15.2 to 1, including the
  15|                       special area and special education teachers, not as an average homeroom size. Our MCAS data
  16|                       from the spring of 2018 indicates we are meeting or exceeding expectations above state averages
  17|                       in the following areas: Grade 3 Reading at 59%, Grade 4 Math at 51%, Grade 5 Math at 47% and
  18|                       Grade 5 Science at 50%. There are teaching teams of 2 at each grade level as well as self-contained
  19|                       classrooms in grades 3 and 4. Special area classes include art, music, PE, library, technology,
  20|                       computer skills, and for 5'h graders, developmental guidance.
  21|                       Teachers are engaging in a variety of professional development trainings. To address physical and
  22|                       mental health concerns there's been training in Trauma, Mindfulness, Epilepsy, and Executive
  23|                       Functioning. To improve literacy, teachers have taken classes in Calkins Units of Study, Reader's
  24|                       Workshop, and Project Read. Math teachers have participated in several hours of preparation in
  25|                       the Everyday Math platform as well as IXL math. A full day of professional development in
  26|                       November was dedicated to computer literacy and software offerings.
  27|                       We offered many after school activities for students in the winter and spring last year. Over 100
  28|                       students signed up for cooking, student council, crafts, paper making, board games, kickball and
  29|                       garden art. We had the Girls on the Run program both in the spring and fall with between 15-25
  30|                       participants and a chess program taught by a chess master which includes about a dozen students.
  31|                       $6100 was raised during our annual Penny Wars event to support funding for a variety of field
  32|                       trips and in-house performances. 5' graders spent a week in Beckett, MA enjoying the Nature's
  33|                       Classroom program. The Bridges program introduced students to several senior citizen volunteers
  34|                        who came in to share their life experiences and learn about the younger generation. The six week
  35|                       program culminated in a walking field trip to the Eagle House to celebrate the bonds that had been
  36|                        created and allow students to tour the senior center. In June they attended a Worcester
  37|                       Braveheart's baseball game at Hanover Park and took in the activities for Baseball in Education
  38|                       Day. In the fall, grade 5 teachers instituted regular walking field trips to the public library every
  39|                       month so students could become familiar with one of Lunenburg's best public resources.
  40|                                                                                              122

   8|                       Southwick Zoo to give 3'd graders an up close introduction to some exotic animals.
   9|                       North End Subaru in Lunenburg once again gifted our school with dozens of non-fiction, high
  10|                       interest titles about science. They include such titles as: This Book Stinks! Gross Garbage, Rotten
  11|                       Rubbish, and the Science of Trash; Try This! 50 Extreme Fun & Safe Experiments for the Mad
  12|                       Scientist in You; and Magnets Push, Magnets Pull. We are grateful for their continued support as
  13|                       well as several other community organizations: the PTO, whose funds allow all students to
  14|                       participate in field trips and financed the purchase of a six month trial program to IXL Learning,
  15|                       the Lunenburg Turkey Hill Family Lions Club who provided scholarships for Nature's Classroom
  16|                       and regularly provides food donations for students at Extended Day, BoxTop collectors and
  17|                       counters, Hannaford Helps supporters, Community Reader day volunteers, parents (both those
  18|                       who support their children at home as well as those who donate hours to school), our Veteran's
  19|                       Day and Memorial Day guests and guest speakers. In December with the blessing of our School
  20|                       Advisory Council, we agreed to participate in the Kylee's Kare Kits for Kids program in
  21|                       Leominster. This offers our students in need weekend bags of food, including winter and spring
  22|                       break and summer vacation. This officially piloted in January 2019.
  23|                       With the addition of a new music teacher in September, we have created a band program for grade
  24|                       five students. There are over 30 students who participate and learn their instruments in sectionals
  25|                       and as part of a full band twice weekly. Their holiday concert in December was a rousing success
  26|                       and included a small but melodic chorus. In the future we hope to expand that program to include
  27|                       4*h graders as well. 3 graders are introduced to instruments through recorder instruction. Students
  28|                       also have the opportunity to participate in an after school music program to learn piano, guitar, etc.
  29|                       As an elementary school we understand that our mission extends far beyond the academic. We try
  30|                       to promote positive and civil interchange and empathy for others. We teach and reinforce coping
  31|                       strategies, self-regulation skills, and calming techniques. We welcome new students and staff
  32|                       who join us throughout the year on our hallway bulletin board. We use age appropriate picture
  33|                       books at each grade to introduce students to diverse cultures and expand their understanding of the
  34|                       world. We teach responsible digital citizenship in an era where soon they will be inundated with
  35|                       social media. We celebrate the positive role models that exist in our school community with
  36|                       student-of-the-month acknowledgements.

   1|                                                                              Lunenburg Middle School
   2|                        Lunenburg Middle School provides a rigorous academic curriculum as well as strong programs
   3|                        that support students' social and emotional growth. These programs ensure that each child
   4|                        becomes a self-motivated, creative, lifelong learners in a safe, stimulating environment that
   5|                        encourages diversity and open honest communication. The dedicated and accomplished staff of
   6|                        professionals within the school embraces the philosophy of educating the whole child
   7|                        academically, socially, and emotionally. This philosophy is a means by which all students become
   8|                        positive community members that possess the skills to be successful in high school and beyond.
   9|                         Lunenburg Middle School is in its third year as a co-located middle- high school serving grades
  10|                        six through eight in a beautiful facility. Our effective middle school model is student centered and
  11|                        provides opportunities to explore a variety of different interests and talents through special area
  12|                        and enrichment classes and extracurricular activities. One of our goals is for students to discover
  13|                        something they are passionate about and want to continue exploring as they move through high
  14|                        school and beyond. We will continue to seek out opportunities for students that foster critical
  15|                        thinking and problem solving skills that prepare them for high school and beyond or what their
  16|                        passion may lead them to.

===PAGE 126=== (ocr, 39 lines)
   1|                       In reviewing the results of the 2018 Spring M.C.A.S. tests, our percentage of students scoring in
   2|                        the meeting or exceeding expectations range remains strong and above the state average in 6 of
   3|                       the 7 tested areas in the middle school. The Department of Elementary and Secondary Education
   4|                        provides an accountability rating for all schools and districts in the state based upon next
   5|                        generation MCAS testing. Lunenburg Middle School accountability rating for 2018 is designated
   6|                        as not requiring intervention, partially meeting goals.
   7|                         Although we are proud of our students' performance, we continue to analyze data in our monthly
   8|                       results faculty meetings designed to improve our instruction for all students. Our faculty has
   9|                       identified areas of improvement based upon the data and implemented strategies to improve their
  10|                        instructional practices that will help students succeed.
  11|                        We continue to utilize intervention and power blocks during the school day to meet the needs of
  12|                        each individual student. These blocks of instructional time that have been built into our master
  13|                        schedule to allow teachers time to work with students at their own individual skill level. The
  14|                        philosophy is to challenge students who are high academic achievers as well as strengthen skills
  15|                       for students who have identified weaknesses. Teachers are able to work with students in a small
  16|                        group to answer individual questions or provide more individualized support. We design this
  17|                       support model to allow students to feel more confident, thus, perform better in the classroom. We
  18|                        will continue to refine our intervention block times to best meet the needs of our students. One
  19|                       option for students during this intervention block is the use of our web based program called IXL.
  20|                       IXL allows students to work at their own skill level, build confidence and moved forward with
  21|                        work that is aligned with the state standards. IXL allows teachers a tool for true differentiation for
  22|                        every student allowing them to work and grow at their own pace and level.
  23|                        Lunenburg Middle School continues to offer enrichment blocks for all students. Enrichment
  24|                        classes provide students a block of time in which they receive instruction in the areas of
  25|                        developmental health and guidance. Students also receive instruction in physical education, art,
  26|                       and music classes that allows them to explore their strengths and talents. Students also have the
  27|                        opportunity to sign up for and participate in band and chorus during this block. This enrichment
  28|                       block is in addition to the traditional special area classes students receive, and this block offers
  29|                        students additional physical movement throughout the day, additional opportunities for hands on
  30|                        activities and more exposure to the arts, theatre and technology throughout the school day.
  31|                        We make a positive impact on the students we serve by offering a variety of different programs
  32|                        developed to promote social and emotional growth, self-awareness, and community service. We
  33|                        will continue to utilize Developmental Design program to deliver our social emotional curriculum.
  34|                        Students meet with teachers in small groups to teach social responsibility and problem solving, as
  35|                        well as developing empathy and promoting positive self-esteem and strong teacher/student
  36|                       relationships. Our social emotional programs have been developed to allow students to showcase
  37|                       their talents and abilities, grow and improve as individuals, and promote community outreach for
  38|                       the younger generation.

   4|                        school. The addition of the foreign language instruction has been well received and the students

   6|                        direct their own learning with a program called Genius Hour. Genius Hour fosters a passion for
   7|                        learning back into the curriculum by having students facilitate their own learning based on their
   8|                        interests.
   9|                        Lunenburg Middle School continues to provide high quality educational services and supports that

  11|                        success is our talented faculty committed to making a positive impact on students, our parents and
  12|                        community who support our teaching and learning, and most of all, our students who inspire us
  13|                        through their commitment to learning. Together we continue to make the difference in the lives of

   2|                                                                                         2018-2019
   3|                        Lunenburg High School has been a hub for academic and social activity in 2018-2019. Teachers
   4|                        continue to provide our students rigorous coursework and hold our students to high standards. Our
   5|                        students meet these challenges through collaboration, self-advocacy, and strong work ethic. All
   6|                        students in grades 9-12 have been issued a Chrome Book and there are wireless capabilities
   7|                        throughout the building. Every classroom and instructional space has an interactive projector and
   8|                        voice-lift capabilities. Our students are fortunate to be in a building that can meet the needs of the
   9|                        215 century learner.
  10|                         During the fall sports season, our students practiced and competed on our three grass fields and
  11|                        new artificial turf field. The youth sports teams in the community were scheduled on the fields,
  12|                        as well. During the fall season, most of our fields were being used from 3:00 pm to 8:00 pm.
  13|                        The winter season has been very busy, as well. The gym and weight room are being used for a
  14|                        large portion of the afternoon and evening by our basketball teams, indoor track and field teams,
  15|                        and students and community members in the Adult Education Program. Additionally, we have
  16|                        athletics teams practicing and competing at: Wallace Civic Center, The Groton School, Nashoba
  17|                        Valley Ski Area, and at Fitchburg High School. Our actors and actresses have been rehearsing
  18|                        since January for the Competitive Class Plays.
  19|                        NEASC ACCREDITATION
  20|                        Lunenburg High School is currently going through the accreditation process. Lunenburg High
  21|                        School is currently working on the five priority areas for the NEASC school growth plan. The five
  22|                        Priority Growth Areas are: Curriculum Maps, Professional Growth/Development, School Civic
  23|                        Engagement, Instructional Practices, and Emergency Response Procedures. The five areas we are
  24|                        currently working on to produce a report for our NEASC accreditation. The final accreditation
  25|                        visit will be conducted in 2020 and will look at how well we are making progress on our growth
  26|                        plan.
  27|                        SCHOOL/COMMUNITY PARTNERSHIPS
  28|                        Throughout the year, Lunenburg High School students are involved in a multitude of fundraising
  29|                        and collection endeavors. In the spring, a canned goods drive will be held and admission to the
  30|                        PowderPuff game will cost two canned goods. Everything collected will be donated to the
  31|                        Lunenburg Food Pantry. Around the holiday season, advisories, LEA, STUCO, NHS and
  32|                        numerous other agencies collected items for the Lunenburg Gift Card Mart Drive.
  33|                        A Senior English class called community service learning component is a class in which students
  34|                        are tasked with researching and identifying needs in the community and then forming an action
  35|                        plan to address the needs. For example, we have students working on: careers that do not require
  36|                        college level degrees. This is to help students make a career choice that does not require a college
  37|                        degree.

===PAGE 135=== (ocr, 47 lines)
   1|                          Schools across North Central Massachusetts are filled with eager students, talented educators and sup-
   2|                          portive admınıstrators, all working together toward common goals: student achievement and academic
   3|                          excellence. While students and teachers at Monty Tech work together toward these goals daily, they
   4|                          also strive to achieve vocational-technical proficiency, assuring our graduates have a choice when they
   5|                          providing the best possible educational programs for our students.
   6|                          Monty Tech academic programs are effectively serving students at all levels, as indicated on the most
   7|                         recent MCAS scores: 95% of students earned Advanced or Proficient scores in ELA, 85% earned Ad-
   8|                          vanced or Proficient scores in mathematics, and 82% earned Advanced or Proficient scores in Biology.
   9|                          Student performance on this exam met or exceeded state-determined targets in every subgroup.
  10|                          Teachers continue to refine curriculum, incorporate new instructional strategies, and challenge every
  11|                          student to reach new levels, and we couldn't be prouder of the results.
  12|                         School leaders also closely monitor each of the school's 21 vocational programs, to ensure they align
  13|                          with current industry standards, and that they continue to prepare students for entry-level careers in
  14|                          their chosen field. Whether it means purchasing new equipment, incorporating new certifications or
  15|                          credentials into the curriculum, or seeking new educational partners, vocational instructors and school
  16|                          leaders work collaboratively to ensure vocational programs at Monty Tech are among the most com-
  17|                          prehensive, current, and innovative programs across the Commonwealth.
  18|                          The 2017-2018 school year was marked by countless reasons to celebrate our students and staff, who
  19|                          consistently demonstrate vocational excellence and innovation.
  20|                          Students and instructors in our Carpentry, Electrical, Plumbing, Masonry, HVAC and Property
  21|                          Maintenance, and Cabinetmaking trades completed a two-year long project - a 7,500 sq. ft. building,
  22|                          now home to the school's newest vocational program, Veterinary Science. This project was funded
  23|                          entirely by private sector donations, gifts, local, state and federal grants, and in-kind support in the
  24|                          form of donated materials and labor, and deep discounts on building materials and supplies. School
  25|                          officials raised an unprecedented $2.6M to support the establishment of the Monty Tech Veterinary
  26|                          Science program - a tremendous accomplishment that reflects the support our community continues to
  27|                          provide our students, faculty and staff.
  28|                          The Monty Tech Veterinary Clinic is not the only new and exciting opportunity available to our stu-
  29|                          dents. The school was recently awarded a $500,000 Skills Capital Grant, to improve the Engineering
  30|                          Technology, Electrical, and CAD/Drafting & Design programs. This generous grant has allowed in-
  31|                          structors to create two innovative learning spaces, intended to replicate working and learning environ-
  32|                          ments maintained by industry leaders in advanced manufacturing and automation. Using this new
  33|                          equipment, students will prepare to become manufacturing technicians, robotics technicians, automa-
  34|                         tion technicians, moldmakers, and CNC machinists at local corporations, filling the existing skills gap
  35|                         across these industries.
  36|                          While students and instructors across the school continue to demonstrate creativity, innovation, and
  37|                          leadership, school leaders continue to keep an eye on emerging trends in vocational education. As we
  38|                          prepare these talented students to make important life choices, we are reminded that in the end, the
  39|                          choice is theirs to make: college or career or both. It is our job to support their aspirations and to edu-
  40|                          cate and train them to achieve at the highest possible level. On behalf of our talented educators and
  41|                          administrators, who remain focused on delivering the highest quality academic and vocational-
  42|                         technical education possible, I am delighted to present the District's 2017-2018 annual report to you,
  43|                          providing a snapshot of the wonderful experiences happening on a day-to-day basis here at Monty
  44|                          Tech.
  45|                          Respectfully submitted,
  46|                          Sheila M. Harrity, Ed.D., Superintendent-Director
