  28|                                                                                     Enrollment
  29|                          On June 1, 2018, student enrollment at Monty Tech included 1,387 students in grades nine through twelve, rep-
  30|                          resenting each of the district's eighteen sending communities. Each class of students is comprised of a relatively
  31|                          equal balance of male vs. female students, and each student attending Monty Tech has elected to do so, prepared
  32|                          to explore an interest in one of the school's twenty-one rigorous vocational-technical programs. While the school
  33|                          currently offers only five programs non-traditional for male students, and twelve programs non-traditional for
  34|                          female students, we are proud to have a student population that is well- balanced by gender and a variety of aca-

  22|                       area students.
  23|                                                                                 Class of 2018 Awards
  24|                       Members of the Class of 2018 were awarded approximately $97,000 in scholarships. The Monty Tech Foundation
  25|                       generously provided $37,250 in scholarships to graduating seniors, ranging in amounts of $100 to $2,600. The
  26|                        Foundation also awarded $3,240 to the Practical Nursing graduates. Once again, local and state organizations, as well
  27|                       as generous individuals, continue to recognize the ability and potential of Monty Tech graduates in the form of
  28|                        financial donations. The School Committee, administration, faculty, and graduates themselves, are grateful for this
  29|                       support.
  30|                        Articulation Agreements with local colleges also play an important role in helping reduce the cost of higher education.
  31|                       Qualified Monty Tech students are eligible to receive college credits through a number of articulation agreements with
  32|                       public and private colleges across the country. Approximately 57% of the graduating class of 2018 reported plans to
  33|                       enroll at a 4-year college/university upon graduation. By earning college credits while still in high school, these
  34|                       students will save both time and money as they pursue advanced educational programs.
  35|                                                                                    Financial Report
  36|                       A great deal of effort was put forth by the School Committee, administration, and staff to develop a cost- effective
  37|                       budget for the fiscal year 2017-2018. The final fiscal year 2017-2018 Educational Plan totaled $26,895,680, which
  38|                       represents a 2.0% increase over the 2016-2017 Educational Plan. The District's FY17 budget exceeds the minimum
  39|                       spending required by Massachusetts General Law Chapter 70 by only $41,379 or .2%.
  40|                       The District was audited in November 2018 as part of the yearly financial audit by the accounting firm of Melanson,
  41|                       Heath and Co. from Greenfield, MA, and received a very good report.

   1|                                                                                   Grants and Contracts
   2|                          Monty Tech continues to pursue grant funding on an annual basis. These funds help provide many educational and
   3|                          social services to the student population. For fiscal year 2018, state and federal grant sources provided the school with
   4|                          $991,611. Programs funded by these grants include: Essential Health Services, Social Intervention and Mediation,
   5|                          Improving Teacher Quality, Special Education Services and Program Improvement, Title I Support, Perkins
   6|                          Occupational Education, and Marine Corp Junior Reserve Officer Training. The District also received more than
   7|                          $508,000 in competitive grants, including a Skills Capital Grant for $495,000 to purchase equipment for the Electrical,
   8|                          Engineering and CAD/Drafting and Design programs, and a grant from the Community Foundation of North Central
   9|                          Massachusetts in the amount of $13,919 to expand the school's continuing education program to include an Oil Burner
  10|                          Technician training program. Using these allocation and competitive funds, the school was able to purchase a variety
  11|                          of instructional technology, equipment, and supplies to enhance the learning experience across both academic and
  12|                          vocational programs.

   1|                          The Cooperative Education Program is an extension of the student's technical education that combines class-
   2|                          room instruction with on-the-job-training. The Co-op Program provides students the opportunity to further de-
   3|                          velop academic, technical and employability skills in an industry work environment. All students are eligible to
   4|                          participate in Co-op Program, provided they satisfy state and school grade, attendance and performance require-
   5|                          ments. All Co-op students have completed the OSHA recognized Career Safe online health and safety course.
   6|                          The Cooperative Education Program is beneficial for both student and employer. For the student, it is a chance
   7|                          to gain on-the job training that improves both their technical and employability skills. Additionally, making in-
   8|                          dustry connections enhances post-graduate employment opportunities. The Co-op Program allows students to
   9|                          Employer benefits include addressing workforce needs in an efficient manner. Coop students provide a pool of
  10|                          temporary and potential full-time employees who are already trained, thus reducing employer training costs. Co-
  11|                          op work hours may be tailored to suit the needs of partnering employers. During school year 2017-2018, approx-
  12|                          imately 25% of qualified students (Juniors and Seniors) earned Co-op placements, working, learning and apply-
  13|                                                                                Student Support Services
  14|                          During the 2017-2018 school year, Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical School District provided spe-
  15|                          cial services to approximately three hundred students - measuring progress of over two hundred students on
  16|                          Individual Education Plans (IEPs) and just under one hundred students adhering to individualized Section 504
  17|                          plans. While the Student Support Services (SSS) Department encompasses special education, the department
  18|                          provides support and is available to all Monty Tech students.
  19|                          The department includes a full-time nursing staff that administers medications, performs state-mandated health
  20|                          screening exams, and provides, when necessary, health information to the special education team for a student's
  21|                          IEP meeting. The department benefits from a full-time school social worker that participates in departmental
  22|                          meetings and assists students who have needs concerning finances, family issues, homelessness, maternity,
  23|                          health issues, and proper food and clothing. The school is also fortunate to have on staff a full-time psychologist,
  24|                          whose role it is to evaluate all students referred for an initial evaluation or who require a three- year re-
  25|                          evaluation. In addition, we have a full-time speech language pathologist, who is available to assist students with
  26|                          disabilities, assess these students and consult with teachers. Our students also have access to the services of a
  27|                          full-time adjustment counselor and part-time school psychologist. All of these individuals are available for
  28|                          scheduled counseling sessions, mental health emergency treatment, medical/mental health re-entry and transition
  29|                          support and services, as well as crisis intervention.
  30|                          The school's Director of Student Support Services oversees the District's Special Education Program, which is
  31|                          reviewed annually in May, in accordance with regulatory requirements. The comprehensive review and evalua-
  32|                          tion are done in collaboration with the Parent Advisory Council, and the results of the evaluation are used to
  33|                          improve the special education procedures and programs in place at Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical
  34|                                                                                          SkillsUSA

  38|                          for our chapter of Skills USA. The students met the challenges of district competitions, performed well at the
  39|                          state level, and prepared for the national conference. They also conducted several community service projects
  40|                          and raised money for various deserving charities. Serving as co-advisors were Michael Forhan, Auto Body
  41|                         Instructor, Anne Marie Cataldo, Early Childhood Education Instructor, and Brad Pelletier, Special Education
  42|                          Instructor. Highlights of the year include:

  46|                               the Annual Fall State Leadership Conference, where they participated in workshops and leadership exercis-

   1|                                                         Monty Tech School of Continuing Education
   2|                          The Monty Tech School of Continuing Education continues to update and add courses that emphasize a com-
   3|                          mitment to excellence by offering affordable, quality, and enjoyable educational experiences. For the Fall of
   4|                          2017, Monty Tech offered 140 classes with 871 registrations, and during the Spring 2018 semester, there were
   5|                          114 post-graduate and continuing studies courses, with 671 registrations.
   6|                          The program is on track to support North Central Massachusetts workforce readiness pipeline with an increase
   7|                          in career and licensure courses.        The students earn industry-recognized credentials, and participate in extern-
   8|                          ships to support the hands on learning component. We continue to increase our small business partnerships,
   9|                          and the number and quality of personal enrichment classes - sewing, knitting, acrylic painting and glass fusing,
  10|                          to name a few. Catalog distribution has more than doubled, from 80,000 to 170,000 copies, and the relatively
  11|                          new online registration feature continues to add value to our students and instructors.
  12|                          Spring 2019 will see an Oil Burner Technician certification prep courses come to fruition. This will provide
  13|                          our community members with a high quality, affordable entry into a viable career pathway. Upon completion
  14|                          of the 120-hour program, students will have the opportunity to sit for the oil burner technician state licensing
  15|                          exam, and begin their work in the oil burner industry.
  16|                         The continued success and sustainability of an adult education program is based on hiring quality instructors
  17|                          and meeting the needs of the community and supporting workforce development. Our goal in the coming year
  18|                          includes increasing our adult education course offerings, with a continued concentration on career programs.
  19|                          Stay tuned for Pharmacy Technician, Medical Billing and Coding, Manufacturing Boot Camp and Apprentice-
  20|                          ship opportunities at the Monty Tech School of Continuing Education.
  21|                                                                        Practical Nursing Program
  22|                          The Monty Tech Practical Nursing Program is designed to prepare graduates to practice safely, ethically and in
  23|                          a caring manner for patients who are experiencing common variations in health status in diverse health care
  24|                          settings. On June 28, 2018, a graduating class of 35 students completed the Practical Nursing Program and
  25|                          entered the nursing profession. The class achieved an initial pass rate of 77%, with 27 of the 35 graduates pass-
  26|                          ing the NCLEX-PN exam. Five graduates are waiting to take their NCLEX- PN exam, and three graduates are
  27|                          expected to retake the examination in the coming months.
  28|                          All of the 2018 graduates are currently employed in the health care profession throughout Massachusetts, and
  29|                          many are working within the eighteen cities and towns of the Monty Tech school district as LPNs in various
  30|                          health care settings, ranging from long term care, sub-acute care to mental health facilities.
  31|                          The Monty Tech Practical Nursing Program continues to develop the "LPN to BSN Bridge" relationship with
  32|                          Fitchburg State University. Several 2018 graduates are pursuing seats in the LPN to BSN program at FSU and
  33|                          will be continuing their education to the Bachelors in Nursing. Many class applicants cited their attraction to
  34|                          Monty Tech as the opportunity to complete a ten-month accelerated program and then bridge to Fitchburg
  35|                          State University.
  36|                         Monty Tech Practical Nursing students are now completing patient scenarios in the Sim Lab on a weekly basis
  37|                          in Terms 2 and 3. The Faculty Sim team has implemented National League of Nursing (NLN) patient scenarios
  38|                          consistent with our curriculum frameworks, and have also utilized the Sim lab setting to instruct students in
  39|                          developing nursing skills that they may not be experiencing in the clinical setting.
  40|                          Instructors have successfully developed and implemented a Maternity Sim lab boot camp where students uti-
  41|                          lize the new simulation models to simulate the birthing process. Student feedback has been positive regarding
  42|                          these new maternity scenarios, stating it better prepares them for an unexpected outcome during a delivery.
  43|                          Substance abuse and the mental health setting job opportunities have increased with more funding being pro-
  44|                          vided to combat the opiate crisis. Having a clinical rotation at AdCare Hospital in Worcester, and performing
  45|                          simulation scenarios involving substance abuse clients, has better prepared our graduates to work in a sub-
  46|                          stance abuse clinical setting, as well.
  47|                                                                            Looking Ahead
  48|                          While the Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical School District educational community is certainly
  49|                          proud of the achievements of our talented students, faculty, and staff, we continue to have an eye toward the
  50|                          future, always committed to improving our vocational and academic programming, strengthening key partner-
  51|                          ships, and maintaining facilities that contribute to student success and achievement. As we look ahead, there
  52|                                                                                              147

===PAGE 148=== (ocr, 48 lines)
   1|                          are a number of programs and initiatives that we expect will have a positive impact on our school and students for
   2|                         years to come.
   3|                          Expand science offerings to include new biomedical courses: For several months, school officials worked to
   4|                         launch an exciting new biomedical science program. Using grant funds, a science lab was renovated, transform-
   5|                         ing it into a biomedical science laboratory, aligned with current industry standards. In addition, one talented in-
   6|                          structor, Mr. Dylan Hager, attended four weeks of intensive teacher training (2 weeks during summer 2017 at the
   7|                          University of San Diego, and 2 weeks during the summer of 2018 at the University of Washington). While Mr.
   8|                          Hager spent weeks preparing this exciting new coursework, school officials purchased the supplies and materials
   9|                          necessary to deliver two rigorous Project Lead the Way courses, Human Body Systems and Principles of Biomed-
  10|                         ical Sciences. These courses, which will be available to students Fall 2018, are expected to engage students in a
  11|                         variety of hands-on learning opportunities in a newly renovated laboratory environment that replicates industry
  12|                          standards. Students will be trained in the safe and effective use of the same tools that professionals in hospitals
  13|                         and laboratories are currently using and will work together to find solutions to real-world problems by analyzing
  14|                          medical histories, reading and interpreting autopsy reports, and understanding basic biology and human physiolo-
  15|                         gy.
  16|                         Celebrate the completion of the school's newest instructional space: For two years, students and instructors in our
  17|                          Carpentry, Electrical, Plumbing, Masonry, HVAC and Property Maintenance, and Cabinetmaking trades worked
  18|                          to complete an incredible project - a 7,500 sq. ft. building, which would become home to the school's newest vo-
  19|                          cational program, Veterinary Science. With construction of this state-of-the-art facility completed during the
  20|                         summer months, school officials celebrated the finished product with local and state officials, donors, and com-
  21|                          munity members who helped bring the innovative animal science program to Monty Tech. While the facility will
  22|                         not be open to serve pets until Fall 2019, Monty Tech Veterinary Science students will work and learn in the new
  23|                         space in the 2018-2019 school year, preparing for a successful opening September 2019.
  24|                          Expand post-secondary and continuing education opportunities: Montachusett Regional Vocational Technical
  25|                          School is home to a very popular evening program that, in recent years, has expanded to include countless work-
  26|                         force readiness programs. A generous grant provided by the Community Foundation of North Central Massachu-
  27|                         setts has enabled school officials to begin developing a new, meaningful workforce training program that will
  28|                          have an immediate and positive impact on regional workforce needs.                        In 2018-2019, an Oil Burner Technician
  29|                          Certification course will be made available to non-traditional students with an interest in pursuing entry-level ca-
  30|                         reers in HVAC trades. This evening program, the only such course in North Central Massachusetts, will include
  31|                         three industry-recognized certification opportunities and will undoubtedly benefit dislocated workers who have
  32|                          been interested in related careers but unable to participate in the required training, due to lack of offerings or high
  33|                          costs associated with similar training programs.
  34|                          Expand the school's marketing efforts: A Monty Tech high school experience is one students must choose, and to
  35|                          ensure that every interested student in our sending district has access to information needed to make sound deci-
  36|                          sions regarding his/her high school experience, it is imperative that the school's marketing efforts are expanded to
  37|                         include a variety of social media platforms. While the school currently hosts an updated website and Facebook
  38|                          page, school officials are exploring adding Twitter and Instagram accounts, in an effort to continue to engage in-
  39|                         terested students and parents.

   2|                        At 9:06 a.m. the Annual Town Meeting was called to order. The Moderator declared warrant properly served
   3|                        and a quorum was declared. After the pledge, the National Anthem was sung by the Lunenburg High School
   4|                        acappella choir. The Moderator reminded the audience to be sure to pick up the handouts available in the hall-

   8|                        the Board of Selectmen for four terms. Paula then thanked Town Meeting members. The School Committee rec-
   9|                        ognized retired Supt. Calmes for her service to the town. At 9:15 a.m., the Moderator went over the ground rules

===PAGE 173=== (ocr, 38 lines)
   1|                        H RESIDENTIAL USES:
   2|                        (1) Accessory Dwelling: A secondary dwelling unit established in conjunction with and clearly subordi-
   3|                        nate to a primary dwelling unit, whether a part of the same structure as the primary dwelling unit or a
   4|                        detached dwelling unit on the same lot. The dwelling shall include a separate, complete housekeeping
   5|                        unit with a separate entrance, kitchen, sleeping area, and full bathroom facilities. Given that it meets the
   6|                        following criteria:
   7|                        (a) The primary building has at least twelve hundred (1200) square feet of floor area.
   8|                        (b) The entire structure used for dwellings shall not occupy more than fifty (50) percent of the lot area.
   9|                        (c) There is at least one (1) off street parking space for each bedroom or efficiency apartment in the con-
  10|                                   verted portion of the structure, which space shall be provided in conjunction with other parking
  11|                                   facilities.
  12|                        (d) There is provision for screening by fencing or landscaping of outside storage areas.
  13|                        (e) No accessory unit shall have a floor area of less than five hundred (500) square feet plus one
  14|                        hundred (100) square feet for each bedroom over one (1).
  15|                        (f) The floor area of the accessory unit shall not be more than thirty (30) percent of the normally habita-
  16|                                   ble floor area of a combination of the dwelling units, after conversion.
  17|                        (g) Each unit shall be a complete and independent housekeeping unit, containing a bedroom or bedroom/
  18|                                   living room combination, bathroom and kitchen or kitchenette and shall have a separate en-
  19|                                    trance.
  20|                        (h) The exterior appearance of the structure shall not be altered except for:
  21|                        [1] stairways and exits required by law,
  22|                        [2] consistent with the original architecture of the structure.
  23|                        (i) The lot and all structures shall be owned in common and one (1) of the units shall be occupied by the
  24|                                    property owner.
  25|                        (i) If the second unit is discontinued and integrated into the original structure design, the owner shall
  26|                                   notify the Inspector of Buildings in writing.
  27|                        (k) No permit for accessory housing granted hereunder shall take effect sooner than one (1) year after
  28|                                   occupancy of the primary dwelling, nor until the owner/petitioner records the authorization in
  29|                                   the applicable Registry of Deeds at his own expense.
  30|                        (1) All permits for accessory housing must be secured before any construction is undertaken.
  31|                        (2) Boarding House: A single-family dwelling where more than two, but fewer than six rooms are pro-
  32|                        vided for lodging for definite periods of times. Meals may or may not be provided, but there is one com-
  33|                        mon kitchen facility. No meals are provided to outside guests.
  34|                        (3) Multi-Family Dwelling: A building consisting of not more than four dwelling units which are attached
  35|                        by common vertical walls and each unit having a separate or combined entrance or entrances.
  36|                        (4) Single Family Dwelling: A detached building on a single lot containing one dwelling unit, or a facto-
  37|                        ry- assembled structure constructed to state building code standards.
  38|                                                                                              173

===PAGE 174=== (ocr, 42 lines)
   1|                        (5) Two-Family Dwelling: A residential structure designed to house a single-tamily unit from lowest
   2|                        level to roof, with a private outside entrance, but not necessarily occupying a private lot, and sharing a
   3|                        common wall adjoining dwelling units.
   4|                        (6) Town House: Single-family attached unit in structures housing three or more dwelling units, con-
   5|                        tiguous to each other only by the sharing of one common bearing or party wall; such structures are to
   6|                        be of the townhouse or rowhouse type as contrasted to multiple-dwelling apartment structures. No
   7|                        single structure shall contain in excess of five dwelling units and each dwelling unit shall have sepa-
   8|                        rate and individual front and rear entrances.
   9|                        I INSTITUTIONAL USES
  10|                        (1) Assisted Living: A special combination of housing, supportive services, personalized assistance,
  11|                        and health care designed to respond to the individual needs of those who need help with activities of
  12|                        daily living. A facility with a central or private kitchen, dining, recreational, and other facilities, with
  13|                        separate bedrooms or living quarters, where the emphasis of the facility remains residential.
  14|                        (2) Charitable Institution: Any entity which: (1) has been certified as a not-for-profit organizations
  15|                              under Section 501(c)(3) of the Internal Revenue code, and (2) has religious, charitable, or elee-
  16|                              mosynary functions or is a religious or charitable organization. As used in this definition, a chari-
  17|                              table organization is an organization which exclusively, and in a manner consistent with existing
  18|                              laws and for the benefit of an indefinite number of persons, freely and voluntarily ministers to the
  19|                              physical, mental, or spiritual needs of persons, and which thereby lessens the burdens of govern-
  20|                              ment.
  21|                        (3) Church: A building wherein persons regularly assemble for religious worship and which is main-
  22|                        tained and controlled by a religious body organized to sustain public worship, together with all acces-
  23|                        sory buildings and uses customarily associated with such primary purpose. Includes synagogue, tem-
  24|                        ple, mosque, or other such place for worship and religious activities.
  25|                        (4) Educational Use: Use of land or a building or buildings as or for an institution not for profit but for
  26|                        the establishment and maintenance of a public or private college, secondary, elementary, trade or vo-
  27|                        cational school or other educational institution for the academic instruction and cultivation of the
  28|                        mind and/or the inculcation of a clearer sense of moral and spiritual values.
  29|                        (5) Hospital: An institution, licensed by the state department of health, providing primary health ser-
  30|                        vices and medical and/or surgical and/or mental health care to persons, primarily inpatients, suffering
  31|                        from illness, disease, injury, deformity, and other physical or mental conditions, and including as an
  32|                        integral part of the institution, related facilities such as laboratories, outpatient facilities, or training
  33|                        facilities.
  34|                        (6) Government Building: Any building held, used, or controlled exclusively for public purposes by
  35|                        any department or branch of government, state, county, or municipal, without reference to the owner-
  36|                        ship of the building or of the realty upon which it is situated. A building belonging to or used by the
  37|                        public for the transaction of public or quasi-public business.
  38|                        (7) Public Utility: All lines and facilities related to the provision, distribution, collection, trans-
  39|                        mission, or disposal of water, storm and sanitary sewage, oil, gas, power, information, telecommuni-
  40|                        cation and telephone cable, and includes facilities for the generation of electricity. Facilities shall be
  41|                        licensed by the Department of Public Utilities (DPU).
  42|                                                                                              174

===PAGE 175=== (ocr, 39 lines)
   1|                        (8) Water Supply: A system for the provision to the public of piped water for human consumption if
   2|                        the system serves 15 or more service connections or which regularly serves 25 or more individuals.
   3|                        The term includes: (a) any collection, treatment, storage, or distribution facility under control of the
   4|                        operator of the system and used primarily in connection with the system; and (b) any collection or pre-
   5|                        treatment storage facility not under the control of the operator of the system which is used primarily in
   6|                        connection with the system.
   7|                        JRECREATION USES
   8|                        (1) Outdoor Entertainment: Any establishment whose main purpose is to provide the general public
   9|                        with an amusing or entertaining activity and where tickets are sold or fees are collected for the activity.
  10|                        Includes, but not limited to, skating rinks, water slides, miniature golf courses, arcades, bowling alleys,
  11|                        and billiard halls, but not movie theaters.
  12|                        (2) Indoor Entertainment: An establishment providing completely enclosed recreation activities. Ac-
  13|                              cessory uses may include the preparation and serving of food or the sale of equipment related to
  14|                              the enclosed uses. Included in this definition shall be bowling, rollerskating or ice-skating, bil-
  15|                              liards, pool, motion picture theaters, and related amusements.
  16|                        (3) Golf Course: A tract of land laid out with at least nine holes for playing a game of golf and im-
  17|                        proved with tees, greens, fairways, and hazards. A golf course may include a clubhouse, restaurant,
  18|                        golf-related retail, restrooms, driving range, and shelters as accessory uses.
  19|                        (4) Private Club: A facility open only to bona fide members and guests of the private organization op-
  20|                        erating the facility. This includes recreational centers for the exclusive use of members and their guests
  21|                        with facilities that may include swimming pools and/or tennis courts, but specifically excluding golf
  22|                        courses.
  23|                        (5) Private Camp: Land under single ownership and management having tents, buildings, or other shel-
  24|                        ters (not including recreational vehicles or mobile homes) for recreational or educational purposes and
  25|                        accommodating four or more people for two or more days, or portions thereof.
  26|                        (6) Recreation: The refreshment of body and mind through forms of play, amusement, or relaxation.
  27|                              The recreational experience may be active, such as boating, tishing, and swimming, or may be pas-
  28|                              sive, such as enjoying the natural beauty of the shoreline or its wildlife.
  29|                        K COMMERCIAL USES
  30|                        (1) Adult Use: Adult uses, as defined by Section 9A of Chapter 40A, provided that:
  31|                        (a) All buildings containing adult uses are at least two hundred fifty (250) feet from an existing re-
  32|                              dence, school or place of worship and are at least five hundred (500) feet from an existing Residen-
  33|                              tial or Outlying District boundary.
  34|                        (b) All parking is in the rear of the setback line and is screened from view of abutting properties.
  35|                        (c)        All signs shall be approved by Development Plan Review and the Planning Board shall review
  36|                                   the size, location, number, design, color and content to determine a public nuisance or be in-
  37|                                   compatible with the character of the community and, as to content, to determine only that the
  38|                                    sign or signs are not obscene.
  39|                                                                                              175

   1|                        (d) All requirements of Section 9A of Chapter 40A are met including that no Special Permit is granted
   2|                                   to a person (s) who have been convicted of violating the provisions of Section 63 of Chapter
   3|                                   119 or Section 28 of Chapter 272 of MGL.
   4|                        (e) The Board of Selectmen may require that a security guard be on the premises during all or some
   5|                                    hours of operation.
   6|                        (2) Auction House: A building, area, or areas within a building used for the public sale of goods,
   7|                        wares, merchandise, or equipment to the highest bidder. This definition excludes therefrom an auction,
   8|                        the principal purpose of which is the sale of livestock or motor vehicles.
   9|                        (3) Bed & Breakfast: Bed and Breakfast, or Bed and Breakfast Establishment provided that:
  10|                        (a) The use complies with the Commonwealth's [MGL 64b Section 1 (a) and/or (b)]definition of Bed
  11|                                   and Breakfast, or Bed and Breakfast Establishment provided the dwelling is owner occupied.
  12|                        (b) The lot conforms to all dimensional requirements of the Zoning Bylaw.
  13|                        (c) Parking for each room available for rent is provided in the side yard behind the setback line or in
  14|                                   the rear yard, but not nearer than ten (10) feet to any property line. One (1) parking place shall
  15|                                   be provided for each bedroom.
  16|                        (d) The outside appearance of the building is not altered except to comply with the Building
  17|                              Code.
  18|                        (4) Drive-in Theater: An open lot or part thereof, with its appurtenant facilities, devoted primarily to
  19|                        the showing of moving pictures on a paid admission basis to patrons seated in automobiles, this does
  20|                        not include Adult Theaters.
  21|                        (5) Hotel: An establishment providing, for a fee, sleeping accommodations, which are generally ac-
  22|                              cessed through a lobby, corridor or internal hallway and customary lodging services, including
  23|                              maid service, the furnishing and upkeep of furniture and bed linens, and telephone and desk ser-
  24|                              vice. Related ancillary uses may include but shall not be limited to conference and meeting rooms,
  25|                              restaurants, bars, and recreational facilities.
  26|                        (6) Laundry Service: A business that provides washing, drying, and/or ironing services for a fee or
  27|                        machines for hire to be used by customers on the premises.
  28|                        (7) Liquor Store: Any business selling general alcoholic beverages, including distilled spirits or hard
  29|                        liquor, beer, wine and malt beverages for off-premises consumption.
  30|                        (8) Medical Clinic: A facility operated by a collected group of physicians, dentists, chiropractors or
  31|                              other licensed practitioners of the healing arts for the examination and treatment of persons solely
  32|                              on an outpatient basis. This is contrasted with an unrelated group of such offices.
  33|                        2) Mixed Use: A combination of commercial and residential uses within a single building or lot. In the
  34|                        case of uses that require a Special Permit, a Zoning Board of Appeals decision must be rendered on
  35|                        the use prior to filing for Planning Board Site Plan Approval.
  36|                        10) Motel: A building or series of buildings in which lodging is offered for compensation, and which
  37|                        is distinguished from a hotel primarily by reason of providing direct independent access to, and adjoin-
  38|                        ing parking for, each rental unit.
  39|                                                                                              176

===PAGE 177=== (ocr, 41 lines)
   1|                         (11) Office Park: A development on a tract of land that contains a number of separate businesses, of-
   2|                         fices, light manufacturing facilities, accessory and supporting uses, and common open space designed,
   3|                         planned, and constructed on an integrated and coordinated basis.
   4|                         (12) Pawn Shop: An establishment that engages, in whole or in part, in the business of loaning money
   5|                         on the security of pledges of personal property, or deposits or conditional sales of personal property,
   6|                         or the purchase or sale of personal property.
   7|                         (13) Personal Improvement Service: A business primarily providing instruction and/or facilities for
   8|                         dancing, martial arts, music instruction, physical exercise, fitness training, or other voluntary physical
   9|                         or mental health services not related to a medical diagnosis.
  10|                         (14) Professional Office: Offices or studios of professional or service occupations or agencies which
  11|                         are characterized by low traffic and pedestrian volumes, lack of distracting, irritating, or sustained

   2|                           A. Special Conditions & Design Standards:
   3|                           (1) Purpose
   4|                          (a) In pursuit of this opportunity and to address this challenge, the Town implements this bylaw and
   5|                           designates this zoning district as Village Center District in order to encourage economic and residen-
   6|                           tial growth that fits the character of the Town.
   7|                           (b) The purposes of the Village Center District are to:
   8|                           [1] Build upon the historic development patterns in the existing village centers to create attractive,
   9|                           walkable neighborhoods;
  10|                          [2] Encourage adaptive reuse of abandoned, vacant or underutilized buildings or structures where
  11|                           appropriate;
  12|                          [3] Allow for a mix of new land uses that are appropriate to both the needs of the community and the
  13|                          scale of surrounding neighborhoods;
  14|                          [4] Provide incentives to develop larger parcels at higher densities and in a coordinated, planned ap-
  15|                          proach;
  16|                          [5] Maintain a consistently high level of design quality throughout the district;
  17|                          [6] Encourage the development of mixed use buildings and campuses that are designed and con-
  18|                           structed in a manner that is contextually sensitive to the existing structures and facilities.
  19|                          (2) Authority

  18|                        § 250-4.9 Water Supply Protection District.
  19|                              A. Purpose. The purpose of the Water Supply Protection District is to promote the health, safety
  20|                                    and general welfare of the community; to protect, preserve and maintain present and potential
  21|                                    sources of water supply and watershed areas for the public health and safety; to protect, pre-
  22|                                    serve and maintain the existing and potential groundwater supply and groundwater recharge
  23|                                    areas within the Town for public health and satety; to preserve and protect the lakes, ponds,
  24|                                    streams, brooks, rills, marshes, swamps, bogs and other water bodies and watercourses in
  25|                                    Town; to protect the community from the detrimental use and development of land and water
  26|                                    within the district; to conserve the natural resources of the Town; to preserve and maintain
  27|                                    the groundwater table and water recharge areas within the Town; and to prevent blight and
  28|                                    the pollution of the environment.
  29|                              B. District delineation.
  30|                              (1) The boundaries of the Water Supply Protection District shall be as follows: Zone I, Zone II,
  31|                                    and Zone III for the Town of Lunenburg, approved by the Department of Environmental Pro-
  32|                                   tection (DEP) according to Map 1, entitled "Water Protection District, revised October,
  33|                                    2009."
  34|                              (2) Where the bounds as delineated are in doubt or in dispute, the burden of proof that the use is
  35|                                    outside the Water Supply Protection District or does not impact the district shall be upon the
  36|                                    owner(s) of the land in question. However, the Building Commissioner retains its authority to
  37|                                    determine final location with regard to said Water Supply Protection District.
  38|                              (3) At the written request of the owners) of the property in question, the Town may engage a
  39|                                    protessional geologist, a certified soil scientist or a registered professional engineer trained in
  40|                                    hydrology to determine the location and extent of a protection area on the parcel in question
  41|                                    and charge the owners) of said parcel for the cost of the investigation.
  42|                               C. Use regulations.
  43|                              (1) The Water Supply Protection District is established as an overlay district to all other districts.
  44|                                    Land in the Water Supply Protection District shall be subject to the requirements of this sec-
  45|                                    tion, as well as to all other requirements of this Zoning Bylaw which apply to the underlying
  46|                                    zoning districts. Uses that are not permitted in the underlying district shall not be permitted in
  47|                                    the Water Supply Protection Districts.

   8|                                      within the Water Supply Protection District, except for single-family dwelling lots on plans

  10|                                (1) Safeguards. Provision shall be made to protect against toxic or hazardous materials discharged
  11|                                      or lost through corrosion, accidental damage, spillage or vandalism through such measures as
  12|                                     provision for spill control in the vicinity of chemical or fuel delivery points, secure storage
  13|                                     areas for toxic or hazardous materials and indoor storage provisions for corrosive or dissolva-
  14|                                     ble materials.
  15|                                (2) Location. Where the premises are partially outside of the Water Supply Protection District,
  16|                                      such potential pollution sources as on-site waste disposal systems shall, to the degree feasible,
  17|                                      be located outside the district.
  18|                                (3) Disposal. For any toxic or hazardous waste to be produced in quantities greater than those as-
  19|                                      sociated with normal household use, the applicant must demonstrate the availability and feasi-
  20|                                     bility of disposal methods which are in conformance with Chapter 21C of the Massachusetts
  21|                                      General Laws and all other applicable laws and regulations.
  22|                                (4) Drainage. All runoff from impervious surfaces shall be recharged on the site, diverted towards
  23|                                     areas covered with vegetation for surface infiltration to the extent possible. Dry wells shall be
  24|                                     used only where other methods are infeasible and shall be preceded by oil, grease and sedi-
  25|                                      ment traps to facilitate removal of contamination.
  26|                                (5) Monitor test wells. Where fertilizers, pesticides, herbicides or other potential contaminants are
  27|                                      to be applied, utilized or stored and in the opinion of the Planning Board are a matter of con-
  28|                                      cern, a groundwater monitoring program shall be established before the special permit is
  29|                                     granted. Such a program shall adequately monitor the quality of the groundwater leaving the
  30|                                      site through the use of monitor wells and/or appropriate groundwater sample analyses.
  31|                                (6) Natural vegetation. No more than 30% of existing natural vegetation on any lot may be dis-
  32|                                     turbed in an underlying residential district, nor more than 50% of existing natural vegetation
  33|                                      on any lot may be disturbed in an underlying nonresidential district.
  34|                                (7) Technical reference. The technical reference to be used to prepare and review plans is
  35|                                     "Guidelines for Soil and Water Conservation in Urbanizing Areas of Massachusetts," 1977,
  36|                                      U.S.D.A. Soil Conservation Service, Amherst, Massachusetts. Specific guidelines to use in-
  37|                                      clude, but are not limited to:
  38|                                (a) Limit grading to only those areas actively undergoing current construction;
  39|                                (b) The smallest practical area of land should be exposed at one time during development;
  40|                                (c) Limit the length of time graded areas are exposed;
  41|                                (d) Provide temporary or permanent stabilization of disturbed areas at the earliest opportunity.
  42|                                      Limit exposure to less than 60 days;
  43|                                (e) Retain and protect as much of the natural vegetation as possible;
  44|                                (f) Permanent improvements such as streets, utilities, storm sewer, vegetated waterways and other
  45|                                     features of the development should be scheduled for installation to the greatest extent possible
  46|                                      before removing the vegetative cover from an area scheduled for building construction;
  47|                                (g) Protect all fill slopes and cut slopes exceeding five feet in height from storm run-off through

  39|                         § 250-4.13 11 Tri-Town Smart Growth District.
  40|                         A. Purpose and authority. The purposes of the Tri-Town Smart Growth District are to encourage smart
  41|                         growth in accordance with the purposes stated in MGL Chapter 40R and to encourage a range of hous-
  42|                         ing types and opportunities which are appropriate in Lunenburg. The objectives include:
  43|                        (1) To promote the public health, safety and welfare by encouraging a diversity of housing opportuni-
  44|                         ties.
  45|                         2) To provide a range of housing choices for households of varying size, incomes and ages and in-
  46|                         crease the production of housing to meet existing and anticipated need.
  47|                                                                                              199

===PAGE 200=== (ocr, 51 lines)
   1|                         (3) To establish requirements, standards and guidelines which will ensure suitable and cost-effective
   2|                         development and a clear, predictable and efficient development review and permitting process.
   3|                         (4) To enable the Town to receive zoning incentive and density bonus payments under MGL Chapter
   4|                         40R and Chapter 40S.
   5|                         B. Definitions. For purposes of this section, the following definitions shall apply. All terms shall be
   6|                         defined in accordance with the definitions established under the enabling laws or this section, or as set
   7|                         forth in the rules and regulations of the permit approval authority ("regulations"), if any. To the extent
   8|                         that there is any conflict between the definitions set forth is this section or the regulations and the ena-
   9|                         bling laws, the terms of the enabling laws shall govern.
  10|                         ACCESSORY USE
  11|                         An accessory use shall be customarily incidental to any of the permitted uses, provided that there is no
  12|                          exterior display and that there are no products sold on the premises and no customers or clients coming
  13|                         to the premises.
  14|                         AFFORDABLE HOMEOWNERSHIP UNIT
  15|                         An affordable housing unit required to be sold to an eligible household.
  16|                         AFFORDABLE HOUSING
  17|                         Housing that is affordable to and occupied by eligible households.
  18|                         AFFORDABLE HOUSING RESTRICTION
  19|                         A deed restriction of affordable housing meeting statutory requirements in MGL c. 184, § 31 and the
  20|                         requirements of Subsection G(5) of this bylaw.
  21|                         AFFORDABLE RENTAL UNIT
  22|                          An affordable housing unit required to be rented to an eligible household.
  23|                         AS-OF-RIGHT PROJECT or PROJECT
  24|                         A development of housing under zoning without recourse to a special permit, variance, zoning amend-
  25|                         ment, or other form of zoning relief. A project that requires approval pursuant to this section shall be
  26|                         considered an as-of-right project.
  27|                         ELIGIBLE HOUSEHOLD
  28|                         An individual or household whose annual income is less than 80% of the area-wide median income as
  29|                         determined by the United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), adjusted for
  30|                         household size, with income computed using HUD's rules for attribution of income to assets.
  31|                         ENABLING LAWS
  32|                         MGL Chapter 40R and 760 CMR 59.00.
  33|                         GARDEN APARTMENT
  34|                         A multifamily residential building of not more than three floors.
  35|                         MULTIFAMILY RESIDENTIAL USE
  36|                         Apartment or condominium units in one or more buildings that contain or will contain more than three
  37|                         dwelling units.
  38|                         PLAN APPROVAL
  39|                         Standards and criteria which a project in the Tri-Town Smart Growth District must meet under the pro-
  40|                         cedures established herein and in the enabling laws.
  41|                         PLAN APPROVAL AUTHORITY
  42|                         For purposes of reviewing project applications and issuing decisions on development projects within
  43|                         the Tri-Town Smart Growth District, the Planning Board, consistent with MGL Chapter 40R and 760
  44|                          CMR 59.00, shall be the plan approval authority, and is authorized to approve a site plan to implement
  45|                         a project.
  46|                         RECREATIONAL USES
  47|                          Active recreational uses, including but not limited to ball fields, and passive recreational uses, including
  48|                          out not limited to walking and bicycle paths. Amusements or motorized uses shall not be considered
  49|                          eligible recreational uses.

   7|                               (2) Underlying zoning. The Tri-Town Smart Growth District is an overlay district superimposed on
   8|                                     all underlying zoning districts. When a building permit is issued for any project approved in
   9|                                    accordance with this § 250-4.13, the provisions of the underlying districts) shall no longer be
  10|                                     applicable to the land shown on the site plan which was submitted pursuant to Subsection L for
  11|                                    such project.
  12|                         D. Applicability of Tri-Town Smart Growth District. In accordance with the provisions of MGL Chap-
  13|                         ter 40R and 760 CMR 59.00, an applicant for a project located within the Tri-Town Smart Growth Dis-
  14|                         trict may seek plan approval in accordance with the requirements of this section. In such case, then not-
  15|                         withstanding anything to the contrary in this Zoning Bylaw, such application shall not be subject to any
  16|                         other provisions of this Zoning Bylaw, including limitations upon the issuance of building permits for
  17|                         residențial uses related to a rate of development or phased growth limitation or to a local moratorium
  18|                         on the issuance of such permits, or to building permit or dwelling unit limitations.
  19|                         E. Permitted uses. The following uses are permitted as of right in the Tri-Town Smart Growth District:
  20|                         (1) Multifamily residential use, including garden apartments, with a density of 22.03 dwelling units per
  21|                         acre.
  22|                         (2) Parking, including surface, garage-under, and structured parking (e.g., parking garages).
  23|                         (3) Open space and recreational uses.
  24|                         (4) Accessory uses customarily incidental to any of the above permitted uses.
  25|                               F. Project phasing. The Planning Board, as a condition of any plan approval, may require a project
  26|                                    to be phased for the purpose of coordinating development with the mitigation required to ad-
  27|                                     dress any adverse project impacts on nearby properties. For projects that are approved and de-
  28|                                    veloped in phases, the proportion of affordable units and the proportion of market-rate units
  29|                                     shall be consistent across all phases.
  30|                         G. Housing and housing affordability.
  31|                               (1) Marketing plan. Prior to granting plan approval for a project within the Iri-lown Smart
  32|                                     Growth District, an applicant for such approval must submit a narrative document and market-
  33|                                    ing plan that establishes that the proposed development of housing is appropriate for diverse
  34|                                    populations, including households with children, other households, individuals, households
  35|                                    including individuals with disabilities, and the elderly. Not less than 10% of the residential
  36|                                     units within a project shall be three-bedroom units. These documents in combination, to be
  37|                                    submitted with a site plan application pursuant to Subsection L below, shall include details
  38|                                     about construction related to the provision, within the development, of units that are accessible
  39|                                    to the disabled.
  40|                              (2) Number of affordable housing units. Not less than 25% of housing units constructed in a pro-
  41|                                    ject shall be affordable housing; provided, however, that the Planning Board may consider an
  42|                                    application where 20% of the units are affordable housing set aside for eligible households. For
  43|                                    purposes of calculating the number of units of affordable housing required within a project,
  44|                                    any fractional unit of 13 0.5 or greater shall be deemed to constitute a whole unit.
  45|                               (3) Requirements. Affordable housing shall comply with the following requirements:
  46|                                                                                              201

===PAGE 202=== (ocr, 52 lines)
   1|                              (a) For an affordable rental unit, the monthly rent payment, including utilities and parking, shall
   2|                                   not exceed 30% of the maximum monthly income permissible for an eligible household, as-
   3|                                   suming a family size equal to the number of bedrooms in the unit plus one, unless other af-
   4|                                   fordable program rent limits approved by the DHCD shall apply.
   5|                              (b) For an affordable homeownership unit, the monthly housing payment, including mortgage
   6|                                    principal and interest, private mortgage insurance, property taxes, condominium and/or
   7|                                    homeowner's association fees, insurance, and parking, shall not exceed 30% of the maximum
   8|                                    monthly income permissible for an eligible household, assuming a family size equal to the
   9|                                    number of bedrooms in the unit plus one.
  10|                              (c) Affordable housing required to be offered for rent or sale shall be rented or sold to and occu-
  11|                                   pied only by eligible households.
  12|                        (4) Design and construction. Units of affordable housing shall be finished housing units. Units of af-
  13|                        fordable housing shall be dispersed throughout the development of which they are part and be compa-
  14|                        rable in initial construction quality and exterior design to the other housing units in the development.
  15|                        The total number of bedrooms in the affordable housing shall be proportionate to the total number of
  16|                        bedrooms in all the units in the development of which the affordable housing is part, provided that at
  17|                        least 10% of the three-bedroom units within the district shall be affordable housing.
  18|                        (5) Affordable housing restriction. Each unit of affordable housing shall be subject to an affordable
  19|                        housing restriction which is recorded with the appropriate Registry of Deeds or District Registry of
  20|                        the Land Court and which contains the following:

  22|                              (b) The name and address of an administering agency with a designation of its power to monitor
  23|                                   and enforce the affordable housing restriction;
  24|                              (c) A description of the unit of affordable housing by address and number of bedrooms;
  25|                              (d) Reference to a housing marketing and resident selection plan, to which the affordable housing
  26|                                   is subject, and which includes an affirmative fair housing marketing program, including pub-
  27|                                   lic notice and a fair resident selection process. The housing marketing and selection plan may
  28|                                   provide for preferences in resident selection to the extent consistent with applicable law; the
  29|                                   plan shall designate the household size appropriate for a unit with respect to bedroom size
  30|                                   and provide that the preference for such unit shall be given to a household of the appropriate
  31|                                   size;

  33|                                    on all subsequent sales and rentals from a list of eligible households compiled in accordance
  34|                                    with the housing marketing and selection plan;
  35|                              (f) Reference to the formula pursuant to which rent of a rental unit or the maximum resale price
  36|                                    of a homeownership unit will be set;
  37|                              (g) Designation of the priority of the affordable housing restriction over other mortgages and re-
  38|                                    strictions, provided that a first mortgage of a homeownership housing unit to a commercial
  39|                                   lender in an amount less than the maximum resale price may have priority over the affordable
  40|                                    housing restriction if required by then current practice of commercial mortgage lenders;
  41|                               (h) A requirement that only an eligible household may reside in affordable housing and that no-
  42|                                   tice of any lease or sublease of any unit of affordable housing shall be given to the adminis-
  43|                                    tering agency;
  44|                              (i) Provision for effective monitoring and enforcement of the terms and provisions of the afforda-
  45|                                    ble housing restriction by the adminıstering agency;
  46|                              (1) Provision that the restriction on an affordable homeownership unit shall run in favor of the
  47|                                    administering agency and the Town of Lunenburg in a form approved by municipal counsel,
  48|                                    and shall limit initial sale and re-sale to and occupancy by an eligible household;
  49|                              (k) Provision that the restriction on an affordable rental unit shall run in favor of the administer-

  51|                                    limit rental and occupancy to an eligible household;

  31|                          § 250-4.14 12 Summer Street Revitalization Overlay District.
  32|                          A. Purpose. The Summer Street Revitalization Overlay District has been established to encourage
  33|                            evelopment that in itself is compatible and aligns with the character of the Town; to create, throug
  34|                            menities, a sense of community that is an appealing place to live and work, ensuring the vision o
  35|                          Lunenburg as a New England Town, and further, to provide clear and precise guidelines as to the
  36|                          building and lot design that will revitalize the area and, when possible, using sustainable building
  37|                          materials and design features that include indoor/outdoor conservation methods.
  38|                           B. Location: in Lunenburg from the Fitchburg line to the Leominster line, including all of the Indus-
  39|                          trial District along Summer Street in Lunenburg and all of the Commercial District along Summer
  40|                           Street and Youngs Road in Lunenburg.
  41|                          C. Objectives:
  42|                          (1) Allowing a mix of uses in close proximity in the district within the development, including resi-
  43|                          dential, retail, office, and light industrial;
  44|                          (2) Preserving and restoring a village-style character to the designated overlay area;
  45|                          (3) Promoting a balance of land uses;
  46|                                                                                              207

===PAGE 208=== (ocr, 46 lines)
   1|                        (4) Promoting the opportunity for people to work, meet, shop, and utilize services in the vicinity of
   2|                             their residences;
   3|                        (5) Providing opportunities for the development of variety of housing opportunities;
   4|                        (6) Providing opportunities for a mixture of uses in the same building;
   5|                        (7) Promoting a positive pedestrian environment in the district;
   6|                        (8) Facilitating integrated physical design;
   7|                        (9) Promoting a consistent level of design quality;
   8|                        (10) Encouraging the development of flexible space for small and emerging businesses;
   9|                        (11) Facilitating development proposals responsive to current and future market conditions;
  10|                        (12)Encouraging the development of open spaces and parks within the district to accommodate
  11|                               workers, residents, pedestrians, and shoppers.
  12|                        D. Permit granting authority. The Zoning Board of Appeals (ZBA) is hereby the review authority per-
  13|                        taining to the Commercial District and where applicable projects proposed within the overlay district
  14|                        shall be reviewed under § 250-8.4, Site plan approval. The Planning Board is hereby the permit grant-
  15|                        ing authority pertaining to the Industrial District where applicable projects proposed within the overlay
  16|                        district shall be reviewed under § 250-8.4, Site plan approvat Special Permit Granting
  17|                        Authority for the Summer Street Overlay District.
  18|                        E. Permitted uses. The following uses are permitted within the Summer Street Revitalization Overlay
  19|                        District:
  20|                        (1) Any use permitted by right or special permit in the underlying zone Uses as outlined in Section 250
  21|                        -4.1.G Use Table.
  22|                        (2) Mixed-use development, which is a development of a tract of land, building, or structure with two
  23|                        or more different uses such as, but not limited to, residential, office, retail, institutional, or entertain-
  24|                        ment. Residential uses shall be allowed as part of a mixed-use project.
  25|                        F. Dimensional standards. These standards herein are hereby established as such to achieve a village-
  26|                        style design for the Summer Street Revitalization Overlay District.
  27|                        (1) Occupied lot area.
  28|                        (a) The total area on any lot devoted to building, parking, outdoor storage, and display and other hard-
  29|                        surfaced areas may occupy up to 85% of the total lot area.
  30|                        (2) Maximum height: no more than 55 feet measured from ground level.

  40|                                     and height that grants plentiful lighting. Such lighting shall shine downward so as to not
  41|                                      affect adjacent properties.

  44|                                     cipal use(s) of the site.

  28|                          § 250-4.15 13 Solar energy systems.
  29|                          A. Purpose. The purpose of this section is to provide siting for solar photovoltaic energy systems for
  30|                          power generation for all home, commercial or industrial installations. Small-scale ground-mounted
  31|                          photovoltaic installations, roof-mounted solar energy installations and large-scale ground-mounted
  32|                          photovoltaic installations within the Solar Overlay District may be constructed without need for dis-
  33|                          set forth herein are met. The provisions in this section of the Zoning Bylaw shall apply to the con-
  34|                          struction, operation, repair, and/or removal of all solar electric systems, and to physical modifica-
  35|                          tions that materially alter the type, configuration, or size of these installations or related equipment.
  36|                          B. Definitions. As used in this section, the following terms shall have the meanings indicated:
  37|                          BUFFER STRIP
  38|                          A strip of land between the solar photovoltaic arrays, and any structures accessory thereto, and the
  39|                          boundary of the parcel, reserved for plant material, berms, walls or fencing to serve as a visual barri-
  40|                          er.
  41|                          LARGE-SCALE GROUND-MOUNTED PHOTOVOLTAIC INSTALLATION
  42|                          A solar photovoltaic system that is structurally mounted on the ground and has a nameplate capacity
  43|                          of 10 kW or greater.
  44|                                                                                              210

===PAGE 211=== (ocr, 51 lines)
   1|                          PLANT MATERIAL
   2|                          Trees or shrubs of a type and height that sufficiently screen the arrays without blocking necessary
   3|                          sun that would hinder the product performance, including ground cover that would screen the lower
   4|                           portion of the arrays.
   5|                          RATED NAMEPLATE CAPACITY
   6|                          The maximum rated output of electric power production of the photovoltaic system in direct current
   7|                          (DC).
   8|                          ROOF-MOUNTED SOLAR ENERGY INSTALLATION
   9|                          Solar photovoltaic arrays placed on the roof of residences, or commercial, industrial or institutional
  10|                          buildings and Town-owned municipal buildings.
  11|                          SMALL-SCALE GROUND-MOUNTED PHOTOVOLTAIC INSTALLATION
  12|                          A solar photovoltaic system that is structurally mounted on the ground and has a nameplate capacity
  13|                           under 10 kW.
  14|                          SOLAR PHOTOVOLTAIC ARRAY
  15|                           An arrangement of solar photovoltaic panels.

   1|                           (i) Hazardous materials. Hazardous materials stored, used, or generated on site shall not exceed the

  11|                           CMR 7.10. The site shall not produce any other vibration, harmonics, or interference which would be

  14|                          arrays, addition to number of arrays or change in placement, made after issuance of the required build-

  18|                           when it fails to operate for more than one year without the written consent of the Planning Board. The
